title: Member Alert: New Handguns Added to California Roster Pursuant to Boland v. Bonta - California Rifle & Pistol Association
content:
For over a decade, California’s Unsafe Handgun Act froze the state’s handgun roster in place. The microstamping mandate, which took effect in 2013, made it virtually impossible for manufacturers to add new semiautomatic pistol models to the Roster of Certified Handguns. The roster shrank year after year. Californians were locked out of the same modern, reliable handguns available to law-abiding citizens in every other state. CRPA refused to accept that. And because of your support, the roster is growing again. Today, September 3, 2026, the California Department of Justice added 25 new semiautomatic handgun models to the Roster of Certified Handguns pursuant to the court’s order in Boland v. Bonta, CRPA’s federal lawsuit challenging the Unsafe Handgun Act. ·         M&P 10mm M2.0 (4.6” and 5.6” barrels, optics ready) ·         Bodyguard 2.0 .380 AUTO (7 configurations) Not a single one of these handguns would be available to California consumers without CRPA’s lawsuit. The full list is available at oag.ca.gov/firearms/certified-handguns/recently-added. In March 2023, Judge Cormac Carney of the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California granted CRPA’s motion for a preliminary injunction, finding that the Unsafe Handgun Act’s microstamping, chamber load indicator, and magazine disconnect requirements likely violate the Second Amendment under the U.S. Supreme Court’s framework in Boland v. Bonta. The court held that these requirements “generally prohibit Californians from acquiring state-of-the-art handguns” that are protected arms under the Second Amendment, and that the State failed to identify any historical tradition justifying those restrictions. The State appealed. The Ninth Circuit partially stayed the injunction, reinstating the chamber load indicator and magazine disconnect requirements while the appeal proceeds, but left the microstamping injunction in place. That injunction is the reason new semiautomatic pistols are reaching the California roster for the first time in over a decade. Following oral argument in August 2023, the Ninth Circuit held the case pending its en banc decision in Duncan v. Bonta. After Duncan was decided in March 2025, the court ordered supplemental briefing, which both sides completed in spring 2025. The appeal is now fully briefed and awaiting decision before the same 11-judge en banc panel. The fight is far from over. The microstamping injunction that opened the door for these new roster additions remains in effect only because of this litigation. If CRPA were not actively prosecuting Boland v. Bonta, the injunction could be dissolved and the roster would once again be frozen. CRPA continues to press for full invalidation of the Unsafe Handgun Act’s unconstitutional restrictions, including the chamber load indicator and magazine disconnect requirements that the Ninth Circuit temporarily reinstated. These requirements continue to block additional handgun models from reaching California consumers. A favorable ruling from the en banc panel would be a generational victory for California gun owners, striking down all three requirements and restoring meaningful access to modern, reliable handguns protected by the Second Amendment. Every new handgun on that roster exists because CRPA had the resources to take this fight to federal court and sustain it for years. Litigation of this magnitude costs hundreds of thousands of dollars. Your donations fund the attorneys, experts, and briefing that make victories like Boland possible. Fullerton, California 92835 The California Rifle & Pistol Association, founded in 1875, provides training in the safe, responsible, and enjoyable use of firearms; sanctions competitive shooting state championships; and fights for the constitutional right to keep and bear arms for those who choose to own a gun in California for sport, hunting, or self-defense. title: Compact SUVs with the most legroom in 2026: Ford Escape tops the list - USA Today
content: What is the second-row legroom of the 2026 Ford Escape? How does the 2026 Toyota RAV4's starting price compare to the Honda CR-V Hybrid? Where can fans stream the East Kentwood vs. Southfield A&T game? The small SUV vehicle segment is one of the most popular vehicle segments in America today because of models like the Toyota RAV4, Honda CR-V and Tesla Model Y. The best-selling small SUVs of recent years are practical and affordable models that function as commuters and family haulers equipped for the needs of a dependable daily driver. When it comes to second-row space, not all compact SUV models are made equally. Some car buyers are looking for the small SUVs with the most legroom for adult-sized and tall passengers. Here's a list of new small SUVs with the most second-row legroom for 2026. The Tucson uses a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine to produce 187 horsepower. It achieves 25 miles per gallon in the city and 33 miles per gallon on the highway. Hyundai's small SUV has a massive cabin. Its second row is roomy enough for adults and tall passengers. The Tucson is affordable and value-oriented. It's one of the best new small SUV options on the market outside of the Honda CR-V and Toyota RAV4. The 2027 Kia Sportage uses a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine to produce 187 horsepower. It earns 25 miles per gallon in the city and 33 miles per gallon on the highway. Kia's Sportage is a close cousin to the Tucson and has near-identical performance specs to its South Korean relative. One of the main differences between the two models is, Kia's small SUV is more affordable than the Tucson. Like the Tucson, the 2027 Kia Sportage has an incredibly roomy second-row of seats. Additionally, it was recently redesigned for the 2023 model year and boasts a modern design language. When it comes to value, the Sportage is tough to beat. The 2026 Honda CR-V uses a 1.5-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine to produce 190 horsepower. It achieves 28 miles per gallon in the city and 33 miles per gallon on the highway. I drove the 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Hybrid model for a week for USA TODAY Cars. It feels agile on the road and it has a practical cabin with decent second-row legroom. Honda's small SUV and its hybrid iteration are two of the best new small SUVs on the market because they're affordable, have enjoyable driving dynamics, and feature cabins and cargo areas spacious enough for the needs of small families. The CR-V is one of the best-selling new vehicles of the year, says Car And Driver. The 2026 Ford Escape uses a 1.5-liter turbocharged three-cylinder engine to produce 181 horsepower. It achieves 27 miles per gallon in the city and 34 miles per gallon on the highway. Ford's small SUV has plenty of powertrain options and lots of second-row space for passengers. The 2026 model year is the final Escape small SUV before the nameplate is discontinued after a 25-year production history. If you're a fan of the Escape nameplate and need a roomy compact SUV that doesn't break the bank, this may be the perfect model for you before its discontinuation. Charles Singh is an Autos Connect Reporter for The Tennessean, part of the USA TODAY Network. Contact him at CSingh@Gannett.com.

title: This Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing Is One Year Old, Already Has Three Owners and an Engine Replacement - autoevolution.com
content:
It may look like it has just left the showroom floor, but the truth is that it has already been through a lot in a year and 4,218 miles. The car was sold new by a dealership in early 2025. Just a couple of months later, in April 2025, the engine was replaced under warranty at the original owner’s local dealer in Albany, New York. The Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing is powered by a 6.2-liter LT4 V8 (or two!) with supercharged firepower, pumping out 668 horsepower (677 metric horsepower) and 659 pound-feet (893 Newton meters) of torque. The high-performance sedan rockets from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 3.4 seconds when it is equipped with the auto box or 3.6 seconds when the manual transmission is involved, like in the case of this car. It takes 11.0 seconds/11.4 seconds for the quarter mile with a trap speed of 132 mph (212 kph) on its way to a top speed of 204 mph (328 kph), which is more than the speed needed by a passenger jet such as the Airbus A321neo for takeoff. The second owner had no complaints about the Cadillac sedan, but traded it in in August 2025, at around 4,000 miles, and the dealership sold it once again. The car that was originally a $129,185 deal, with over $32,000 worth of options, in 2025. Now, it has just sold on Cars and Bids for $104,350, and "Blackwing Bill," whoever this guy with a celebrity nickname may be, handled the deal. So what did the buyer get? This 2025 Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing Precision Package rocks Drift Metallic over a Sky Cool Gray and Jet Black interior. The model comes with the Precision Package, which brings stiffer springs and a thicker stabilizer bar. Carbon ceramic brakes provide the stopping power, while track-focused Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 R tires wrap the 19-inch wheels. The sedan also features a limited-slip differential and Magnetic Ride Control suspension. The buyer went home with a still-new car, two keys, and the owner's manual. The Carfax report shows no accidents or mileage discrepancies in the Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing’s brief past. The dealer reports no significant modifications. However, that rear spoiler looks like it is an aftermarket add-on. Elena started off as a sports reporter and five years later switched to automotive. How does that happen? Lots of writing, testdrives, traveling, off-road driving courses, track driving courses, defensive driving courses and diplomas. The diplomas might be "useless", but the knowledge she gained is priceless.

title: We want Fury v Joshua at Wembley - London mayor - sports.yahoo.com
content: London Mayor Sadiq Khan says he is "really keen" to host the proposed Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua fight at Wembley Stadium and has urged promoters to get in touch. BBC Sport understands Saudi organisers Sela have contacted the mayor's office in recent weeks about bringing the long-awaited contest to the national stadium. However, with organisers and broadcaster Netflix understood to favour New York's Madison Square Garden for a November bout, sources close to the discussions say talks over a London venue have not progressed, with no detailed talks over dates or timings. "A message to the promoters - we want to host it in London. Talk to us, we're really keen to have it," Khan told BBC Sport on Thursday. Wembley Stadium's usual curfew is 23:00, although Khan has previously indicated he would support efforts to bring the fight to London. A late-night fight in London - potentially in the early hours - could mean it draws a larger television audience in the US. Brent Council, the local authority involved in any approval, has said a potential extension of the curfew would need to be assessed by Wembley's safety advisory group. It remains unclear how late that curfew could be pushed back. "Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury are two great British boxers. Both have been world champions," Khan said. "They both recognise and love the fans in this country who have supported them throughout their careers, amateur and professional. "Wembley has hosted many fantastic events, including bouts involving Tyson and Anthony. We, the fans, want to see them box live in London." There is hope that the venue will be finalised in the coming days. Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn has said he wants an announcement this week, with a news conference to follow next week. Fury calls Joshua a 'coward' as wait for announcement continues Hearn says his side signed a contract for the bout to take place in the United Kingdom, while Sela and Netflix's preference would be the United States, to cater for American audiences. Matchroom Boxing's Hearn has previously said Joshua's contract specifically stipulated a UK venue and would need to be renegotiated for the fight to take place Stateside. Hearn says he has since set out terms under which Matchroom would agree to the change, with negotiations continuing over a possible move to New York. The contact from Sela represents a significant development from the end of July, when sources close to the mayor told BBC Sport there had been no approach from the fight's organisers. But the lack of progress since that initial contact underlines the uncertainty still surrounding Wembley's chances of hosting the contest. "I'm hoping the promoters understand that not only will you get 100,000 people watching this bout live, you'll get millions watching it across the globe, where both boxers are cheered on by their loyal fans," Khan said. Hearts show signs of life, then capitulate to cardiac cats Charlotte at the death After a tough first half in which Portland Hearts of Pine could hardly find the ball and went down 1-0 thanks to a Jon Bakero goal, Hearts managed to rally in the second to net two goals to claim the lead. The tenuous lead would hold all the way into stoppage time, where supersub Stefano Pinho would score a wonder-scissor-kick and a close-range game winner in the dying moments. Out of the gate, Hearts pressured very high and hard, forcing Charlotte's keeper to take action twice. After the first couple of minutes, though, the league leaders settled into the match, holding almost all possession. Slowly, they drove Portland deeper and deeper into their own half and eventually forced Morse into his first big save of the match in the ninth minute. Under consistent pressure, Bobby Murphy could be heard shouting at line leaders Tyler Huck and Diego González "Higher Tyler, higher! Diego, higher!" in an attempt to push the Jacks back into their own half and relieve pressure on their own back line. Though Portland had a couple of opportunities – one through newly returned Lagos Kunga (who started in place of Ollie Wright at attacking midfield), who showed nice dribbling technique to nearly create a shot for himself — most of the first half ran through Jon Bakero, creating near-assists and finishing a play off to net his sixth goal contribution in two games in the 20th minute. Hunter Morse and Diego Letayf both managed to make excellent stops in the 24th and 41st minutes, respectively, preventing a dangerous 3v1 attack from showing its teeth and clearing a ball off the line after a scramble in the box took Morse out of the play. Out of the break, Portland had clearly regrouped, showing an ability to hold onto the ball and keep the possession split relatively even. This manifested in a 52nd-minute chance where Tyler Huck was only just barely beaten by the keeper to a ball after a low cutback to the six-yard box. In the 58th minute, Wright and Camara would enter the field. Their presence immediately brought not only urgency but intent to the possession Hearts couldn't quite find through the first 13 minutes of the half. Their impact and ability to bring others into the game led to a goal not a minute later when Matteo Kidd scored his second of the year on an All-Hustle play. Multiple dangerous chances and rousing possession led to Ollie Wright earning a penalty kick, which was turned into the net off the rebound by Michel Poon-Angeron in the 65th minute. Unfortunately, that would be the end of the Boys of Maine's second-half dominance. The entry of Christy Manzinga, Javen Romero, and former MLSer Stefano Pinho just before the hydration break made all the difference, showing off in a one-touch passing sequence that Hata had to clear out of a dangerous spot. Manzinga's dangerous 1v1 skills culminated in a handful of massive saves by Morse to hold onto the tenuous lead. Ollie Wright very nearly extended Portland's lead two minutes into the announced seven of stoppage time after hitting a beautiful curler, but that would be the last of his team's chances as Charlotte would get an incredibly finish from Pinho (seriously go watch the clip linked in the key moments below), and suspended their panic enough to create one final opportunity to bend Portland past their breaking point and steal not just one but all three points to hold onto their lead at the top of the table. Head coach Bobby Murphy makes four changes from the past weekend's game against Fort Wayne. Diogo Barbosa, Felipe, Aboubacar Camara, and Konstantinos Georgallides all make way for Letayf, Huck, Kunga, and Gonzalez. Kunga returns for his first start since July, while Wright begins the match on the bench. 9' CLT 0-0 POR: Save! Bakero gets slipped in and has a rip, forcing Morse into a save that roused both the fans in-stadium and the commentator team. 16' CLT 0-0 POR: Chance! Lagos Kunga dribbles through a couple players on the right hand side near the box and nearly puts together a dangerous opportunity! 20' CLT 1-0 POR: Goal, Charlotte. Bakero receives the ball in tight traffic and one-times it further across his body further into the far post netting. 24' CLT 1-0 POR: SAVE! After a Hearts corner, Charlotte steal the ball away, having a 3-1 counter that ends with Hunter Morse coming off his line to make a massive save 41' CLT 1-0 POR: Off the line! Morse couldn't get full grip on the ball put in, sending the box into a scramble. A shot gets sent toward goal, but Diego Letayf is there to clear the ball off the line! 52' CLT 1-0 POR: Chance! Tyler Huck, after hustling in the box, is only barely beaten by Charlotte's keeper to claim a ball that was cut back to the six-yard box. 58' CLT 1-0 POR: Subs. Kunga and Huck off for Wright and Camara. 59' CLT 1-1 POR: GOAL! Matteo Kidd outhustles his man and slides the ball past the keeper after Eiji Hata beats his man to rip in a cross from the left touchline! 61' CLT 1-1 POR: Chance! Gonzalez strikes a ridiculous on-target half-volley from the top of the box, but it's near the keeper, who manages to grab hold of the ball. 63' CLT 1-1 POR: PENALTY! After Ollie Wright dances past a couple of defenders, he's taken down in the box by the keeper, who is attempting to push the ball away and wide. 65' CLT 1-2 POR: GOAL! Wright takes the PK low and to his right, but doesn't put it far enough toward the post. The keeper parries out, but Poon-Angeron is first to react and slips the ball into the net to claim the lead! 76' CLT 1-2 POR: SAVE! A deflected shot by Charlotte puts the ball at super close range by Portland's left post for Marou, but Morse sticks his left hand up in rapid fashion to knock the shot away. 79' CLT 1-2 POR: Save! Charlotte's Manzinga feeds a tough cheeky cutback, but it's Hunter Morse again there to make the save - this time on the ground at close range. 87' CLT 1-2 POR: DEEP BREATH. Skinner puts in a cross to Marou who has an open header from 3 yards and nearly turns it in, but the ball sails just over the bar. Afterward, he was deemed offside, though this was the Independence's most clear-cut chance of the match so far. 90+1' CLT 1-2 POR: SAVE! Jon Bakero puts in a free kick that's headed down by Romero, but Morse gets down quickly, claiming the ball just before he hits the ground. 90+2' CLT 1-2 POR: CHANCE! Ollie Wright drives forward and puts in a curler seemingly destined for the top right corner, but it goes just over and wide. So close! 90+6' CLT 2-2 POR: Goal. Romero hits a hopeful cross from the left. Stefano Pinho hits an incredible kinda-sorta scissor kick that finds the back of the net. 90+7' CLT 3-2 POR: Goal. A Bakero long ball from deep is headed on and turned into the near side netting by Pinho to complete a come-from-behind victory at the death. Winless in Nine: Head Coach Bobby Murphy's gotta be feeling the heat under his seat. Losing concentration and conceding two goals deep into stoppage time, Portland managed to drop not just the win but the result altogether. This match brings their in-league winless run to nine games (last win: July 3, 2-1 vs FC Naples) After an excellent debut season, the Boys of Maine now sit 10 points out of the playoffs with 8 games to play. Most other clubs have a game in hand on Portland. Though the team is beginning to look more cohesive after integrating new talent, it's looking like it'll take a small miracle to make the postseason. Wrighting the Ship: Despite the doom and gloom, there are some things to build on from this match. Away from home at the league leaders – including the frontrunner for the USL1 Golden Boot (Marou) and Golden Shoe (Bakero) - no one would have expected Portland to hold a lead right until the last couple of minutes of stoppage time. Last night's match marked the first time Hearts of Pine managed to score multiple goals in a game since August 1 in a 3-3 draw with Greenville Triumph  and neither came from usual starters Ollie Wright or Abu Camara, who were rested and came off the bench. Those two – Camara and more importantly Wright – also showed how the team can still control games against the best for spells. Immediately after entering the match, their quality was impactful, holding possession and looking more purposeful with it. Their presence and vision on the ball instantly brought guys like Hata and Poon-Angeron more into the game, amplifying the team's strengths. Gents Gelling: Fully knowing their increasingly dire position, Portland did add a few talent players this summer, bringing in Diego Letayf, Felipe Rodriguez, and Eiji Hata while Lagos Kunga just returned from an extended absence. The team is starting to look more and more cohesive, with evident talent showing in flashes from all four additions. If Hearts can stay healthy and get their best players on the field to build chemistry with the new additions, they'll have a shot at making a run up the table, even if it might be too late. For nothing else, picking up wins for their fans who continue to show up in droves each and every game is worth the effort. Who else but Hunter Morse? Without the Brick Wall himself, Portland surely would have found themselves buried by a multi-goal deficit long before stoppage time. Though their scrambling defense was OK, Morse's six saves were critical. He continues to lead the league in total saves. Share it with friends and help reliable news reach more people. title: The Burden of Proof in Certified Mailing: Analyzing Wales v. Commissioner and Jurisdictional Thresholds - Current Federal Tax Developments
content: A site devoted to articles on current developments in federal taxes geared toward CPAs in tax practice. Wales v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-82, (Sept. 3, 2026) In the practice of tax controversy, few issues are as critical as the precise boundaries of the United States Tax Court’s jurisdiction. Under the Internal Revenue Code, key deadlines for seeking judicial review are strictly triggered by the administrative mailings of the Internal Revenue Service. A recent decision by the Tax Court, Dania Wales v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, T.C. Memo. 2026-82, highlights a severe evidentiary pitfall for the IRS and provides tax professionals with a powerful precedent for defending taxpayer access to judicial review when the government fails to document its mailings meticulously. The dispute in Wales arose from a Form 8857, Request for Innocent Spouse Relief under I.R.C. § 6015, which the petitioner mailed to the IRS on August 29, 2023. Having received no administrative response or notice of determination from the IRS for over two years, the petitioner filed a Petition in the Tax Court on December 5, 2025, seeking a de novo review of her innocent spouse claim under the statutory “six-month rule.” On January 27, 2026, the IRS filed a Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Jurisdiction, asserting that the petition was untimely. The IRS contended that it had issued and mailed a Notice of Final Determination via certified mail to the taxpayer’s last known address on or before February 4, 2025. If true, this mailing would have triggered a strict 90-day filing window under I.R.C. § 6015(e)(1)(A)(ii), which would have expired in May 2025, rendering the petitioner’s December 2025 filing late. To support its motion, the IRS produced the following documentary evidence: The tracking logs showed that on February 4, 2025, a delivery notice was left at the petitioner’s address because no authorized recipient was available. Subsequent logs showed a reminder on February 9, 2025, and that the mail arrived back at a regional USPS facility on March 6, 2025, before being picked up by the IRS at its Covington, Kentucky facility on March 17, 2025. Crucially, the physical envelope produced by the IRS bore “presorted first-class mail” postage and had “no stamp or sticker indicating it was sent by certified mail.” Furthermore, the IRS admitted that its certified mail log, USPS Form 3877, was entirely unavailable and could not be produced. As the Tax Court emphasized, “The Tax Court is a court of limited jurisdiction and can exercise its jurisdiction only to the extent provided by Congress.” Under I.R.C. § 6015(e)(1)(A), a taxpayer seeking innocent spouse relief may petition the Tax Court “to determine the appropriate relief available to the individual under this section.” The timing requirements are governed by two alternative statutory paths. Under I.R.C. § 6015(e)(1)(A)(i), a taxpayer may petition the Court after the earlier of: If the IRS properly mails a Final Determination Notice by certified or registered mail, I.R.C. § 6015(e)(1)(A)(ii) mandates that the taxpayer’s petition must be filed “not later than the close of the 90th day after the date described in clause (i)(I).” The Court observed that “As in deficiency proceedings, see I.R.C. § 6213(a), our jurisdiction here is also predicated upon the filing of a timely petition.” If the IRS fails to issue a notice, or fails to prove it mailed the notice via certified or registered mail, the taxpayer is free to petition the Court at any time after the expiration of the six-month administrative wait period under subclause (II). Because the petitioner’s Form 8857 was filed in August 2023 and her petition was filed in December 2025, the petition was timely under subclause (II), unless the IRS could prove that its February 2025 notice was dispatched in accordance with the strict statutory requirements of subclause (I). Under established Tax Court precedent, “Respondent bears the burden of proving proper mailing of the Final Determination Notice by competent and persuasive evidence” (citing Coleman v. Commissioner, 94 T.C. 82, 90 (1990)). This requires showing that the notice was “properly delivered to the USPS for mailing” (citing Cataldo v. Commissioner, 60 T.C. 522, 524 (1973)). In typical tax controversy cases, the IRS establishes a presumption of mailing by presenting a properly completed USPS Form 3877 (Firm Mailing Book For Accountable Mail). “A Form 3877 reflecting Postal Service receipt represents direct documentary evidence of the date and the fact of mailing” (citing Coleman, 94 T.C. at 90). Without this form, the presumption of proper mailing does not arise (citing Rivas v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2017-56). However, the IRS argued that the absence of a Form 3877 is not fatal to its case. The Commissioner asserted that “the act of mailing a notice can be proven by documentary evidence or evidence of IRS mailing practices corroborated by direct testimony.” Under this line of reasoning, the IRS requested that the Court infer certified mailing from its secondary tracking data, the tracking number printed on the notice, and the fact that the letter went unclaimed and was returned. The Tax Court flatly rejected the IRS’s arguments, finding that its secondary evidence fell far short of establishing a certified or registered mailing under I.R.C. § 6015(e)(1)(A)(i)(I). First, the Court pointed out the facial contradiction on the physical envelope itself: “The envelope indicated only that the Final Determination Notice was sent via presorted first-class mail” and “bears no stamp or sticker indicating it was sent by certified mail.” Second, the Court scrutinized the electronic tracking data and USPS certification. Although the tracking number on the notice matched the USPS Tracking Plus logs, “The USPS Tracking Plus Statement, however, fails to indicate whether the contents of the letter were sent by certified or registered mail.” The Court noted that “the tracking number itself does not indicate that it was sent via certified or registered mail.” Third, the certification provided by the USPS paralegal was similarly defective because it “fails to state whether the Final Determination Notice was sent by certified or registered mail.” The Court contrasted the IRS’s deficient evidence with standard methods of proving mailing in the absence of a Form 3877. For instance, in Garrett v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2016-179, the IRS produced a “certified mailing list” stamped and initialed by the postmaster. In Crain v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-97, proper mailing was shown through a “computerized certified mailing list which provided equivalent information to Form 3877.” Because the IRS’s record in Wales lacked these standard controls, Judge Weiler held: “On the basis of the evidence before us, we find that the record fails to establish that respondent properly mailed the Final Determination Notice by certified or registered mail. See I.R.C. § 6015(e)(1)(A)(i)(I).” Consequently, because the IRS failed to prove the statutory certified mailing, the 90-day filing deadline was never triggered. The Court concluded: “Since respondent has failed to establish proper mailing... and petitioner filed her Petition more than six months after she filed her innocent spouse election, we hold that this Court has jurisdiction over this case.” The IRS’s motion to dismiss was denied. The ruling in Wales highlights a striking equity in tax controversy. While the IRS was held to strict proof of certified mailing to terminate a taxpayer’s right to petition, taxpayers are held to an equally demanding standard when trying to prove timely filing under I.R.C. § 7502 and Treasury Regulation § 301.7502-1. Under the “mailbox rule” of I.R.C. § 7502, a document is deemed filed on the postmark date if it is received late but postmarked within the prescribed period. However, the taxpayer assumes the risk that a standard postmark may be illegible or that the document may be lost entirely. To eliminate this risk, Treas. Reg. § 301.7502-1(c)(2) provides that taxpayers may use certified or registered mail. Crucially, the regulation dictates: “If the document or payment is sent by U.S. certified mail and the sender’s receipt is postmarked by the postal employee to whom the document or payment is presented, the date of the U.S. postmark on the receipt is treated as the postmark date...” Furthermore, under Treas. Reg. § 301.7502-1(e)(2)(i), a postmarked certified mail sender’s receipt constitutes the exclusive means of proving delivery if the IRS claims it never received the document. The regulation states: “Other than direct proof of actual delivery, proof of proper use of registered or certified mail... are the exclusive means to establish prima facie evidence of delivery of a document to the agency, officer, or office... No other evidence of a postmark or of mailing will be prima facie evidence of delivery or raise a presumption that the document was delivered.” Just as a taxpayer cannot rely on standard USPS tracking printouts or self-serving declarations to prove certified mailing and raise a presumption of delivery when the IRS loses a return, Wales confirms that the IRS cannot rely on tracking histories and tracking numbers to establish certified mailing when it loses its Form 3877 and mails a notice in a first-class envelope. For CPAs, EAs, and tax attorneys representing clients in innocent spouse or deficiency proceedings, Wales provides a critical blueprint: Ultimately, the Tax Court’s decision represents a victory for fairness, establishing that the IRS must be bound by meticulous certified mailing rules similar to those that it imposes on taxpayers. title: Cadillac V-One Concept Engineer Spills the Secrets of a Customer-Spec Le Mans Hypercar - The Drive
content:
We have updated our Privacy Policy. Please review to learn more. By continuing to use our services, you agree to these updates. Published				

					Sep 3, 2026 3:42 PM EDT Our free daily newsletter sends the stories that really matter directly to you, every weekday. Ask the nice folks at Cadillac about this slick prototype race car displayed at The Quail during Monterey Car Week, and they’ll tell you over and over again that it’s just a “design study,” a “concept,” a “race car project.” Ask folks who have their ears on the ground at paddocks across the globe, and they’ll tell you that the program to sell these simplified Le Mans racers to customers is just about finalized. That’s the best way to describe this beauty that Cadillac calls the V-One: an 830-horsepower, simplified Le Mans Hypercar—capital H because the real deal races in WEC’s Hypercar class (and IMSA’s GTP). And regardless of whether General Motors plans on selling these to a wider audience or just a select few—or even just one person like Porsche did for Roger Penske—the task of dumbing down one of the world’s most advanced race cars is no small feat. There’s the engine side, the hybrid side, the electronics, suspension, downforce, maintenance intervals that could quickly bankrupt a very wealthy person, and, last but not least, selling a vehicle that 99.9% of people don’t have the skills to drive is a challenge in and of itself. And for those who do have the skills, then there’s the problem of where do you drive it, and how big of an army of engineers do you need to operate it? Where do you store it, and how do you prep it to make sure it starts up again later? I spoke with Sean O’Shea, the lead propulsion engineer for Cadillac Racing and GM Motorsport’s hybrid powertrains, to get all of those answers and then some. He and I had the chance to explore the V-One up close and learn about what makes this project so ambitious, but also so exciting. Here’s how Cadillac is building a Le Mans Hypercar that anyone can jump in and drive: Jerry Perez: I know the official company line is that this is a concept, but what is Cadillac really trying to achieve here? Is the goal to just make a concept that never goes anywhere, or something that will become a reality? And how are you involved in all of this? Sean O’Shea: As the engineering representative linking the design and the racing program, I’m really trying to make sure that [V-One] doesn’t stray too far from the race-car side and that this could be a reality. It’s a concept now, but everything you see here is very feasible and could be a reality. I’m a big racing guy; I’ve been racing everything since I was little, like go-karts, cars, dirt bikes, all of it. I love racing, so when I got involved in the project, I wanted to make a track car that was a simplified version of our race car, but still had all the same tools and the same experience you would get as a pro driver, without being overly complicated. Race cars are known for being complicated, so how do you take a Le Mans racer and make it less complicated? Well, first, I want it to be a really fun track car, and one of the major details is that it needed to be an “ambient start car,” right? This means you can start it at 70 degrees and let it warm up on its own without having to pre-warm it [with auxiliary machinery like an F1 car]. Also, all the differential, traction control, and suspension are a simplified version of the real car. This means you can just go out and just drive the car and have a really good time. However, I didn’t want to take away from the sound, the power, or the downforce you have in a real race car. This way, when you get in it and look around, you get the same view as any of our pro drivers like Earl Bamber, Jack Aitken, or Delatraz. You’ll also have the same buttons around the cockpit, but maybe not all 12 control variations or whatever, right? That’s what I mean by the simplified version: something we mortals can learn, work through, and have a good time with. I once spoke with Jenson Button while he was racing the Acura ARX at the Rolex 24, and he flat-out told me that the steering wheel and some of the controls of the GTP car—as well as the rear axle, brake balance, and traction control—were more complicated than in an F1 car from his era. If he is saying that, I can’t imagine what a normal person would say. We had Jenson drive the [WEC] car, and yeah, the race car project is so complicated given what they want to accomplish. Between settings, energy recovery, and energy per lap, I worked with our pro drivers and just asked them: what would you like to simplify in the car if you wanted it to be fun? They gave me a lot of ideas, so if you look at the interior, it’s just an LMDh car, just a simplified version of it. We still have traction control with two settings—X and Y for lateral and longitudinal grip—and we really wanted to put ABS in the car, although these cars normally don’t have it. I wanted ABS to kind of eliminate the issues around break-in temperatures, tire warm-up procedures, and all of that. Just let the ABS handle it, then let the driver go out and learn to steer, shift, and go fast. We worked closely with the [pro] drivers to understand how we can reduce complexity. And on the propulsion side and differential side, we worked with all of our performance engineers to, again, learn how to simplify things. We went to Goodwood last year and this year, and it was like, how can the car be easy to use? You know, we started just kind of throwing calibration ideas out there, so that our driver could just basically drive out of the paddock and drive onto the track and not have a team of engineers with them. If you were to build this, would the driver just jump in and go? The idea would be that we jump in, start it, and go. Well, you have to let it warm up before you go anywhere, you know, give it a little care. This is expensive, after all. Would customers keep their cars at home, or would Cadillac store and transport them to tracks, as Ferrari does with its FXX program? We have ideas and a kind of plan, but it’s nothing we’re ready to divulge yet. But for me, being just an enthusiast, if I bought this, I would want to keep it at home and impress my neighbors. Who all has driven the V-One, and what’s their feedback so far? Our pro drivers are in it since this is really close to the race car. We engineers don’t really drive it at all. I’ve been in the seat and pushed it around on EV drive, but nothing more than that. I really draw on their experience because they also drive our road cars; they’ve helped with the ZR1X programs, and they spend a lot of time in the sim rig. Together, we really looked at the interior [cabin] space and explored how to make it a little bigger. So I was like, can we remove the sway bars? And they were like, no, we need adjustable sway bars. I said, okay, but do you just need the rear and not the front? And the drivers were like, you need both—so we kept both. That type of stuff. Which buttons did you keep on the dash and steering wheel, and what about the air conditioning? Yes, there’s AC inside the car. The race car gets very hot, so we knew we wanted to keep that. There’s also pit lane limiter and other buttons to adjust various settings we already discussed. You kept the loud bang from the transition from electric to ICE, like the race car when leaving pit lane, right? Right, we didn’t want to change any of that. Plus, these things are miserable at slow speeds, so it’s much easier to maneuver the car on electric power; then you can just drive around. Again, the idea is to make it simple to use. Start the car, let it warm up. When you pull out of the pits, the ICE engine shuts off, and you leave in EV. Then you let one of the paddles go, and it turns the ICE engine on, and you go. The interior, really. It’s the biggest change from the race car. We just want to make sure that we had space for a normal-sized human in there. And also visibility, because the race car is very claustrophobic. And we had to do all this without changing the tub shape, because if you change the tub, now you gotta make new tooling and homologate everything else. After that, it was just simplifying all the sensors and electronics. Whenever a car company announces an “F1 car for the road,” it usually ends up rather messy. Whether it’s the McLaren F1, the Mercedes-AMG One, you name it, they’re awesome, but they’re full of gizmos and maintenance and reliability nightmares. I know this isn’t an F1 car, but pretty darn close. Never driven an AMG One, but I’ve seen a lot about it, including on the forums. But to me, the complication just isn’t necessary. The core experience for me is being in the car, just having a good time, feeling the downforce, feeling the Gs, hearing the sound, and racing the car on a track. So, for everything we did here, I just wanted to simplify the race car and make it reliable and easy to use. The whole point is to give the owner the experience of driving the car, not to mess with gizmos, gadgets, screens, and everything else. Drive the car! What are maintenance intervals like on one of these? Anytime we do a performance car, anything inside GM, we start with a vehicle technical spec. So you put in what you want the car to do. right? Do you want to have good fuel mileage?  Do you want to have faster 0-60 or lap times, all that stuff? When I did the vehicle technical spec for this, we targeted a lap time—it was a little bit slower than in the race car, and I targeted our performance interval, which is our highest in GM, to 24 hours of just changing tires. So, for 24 hours of racing, just add fuel, change tires, and go. If you want to go out and run 24 hours, that’s what the car will need. Lastly, how will you gauge whether a potential customer can handle a V-One? Can someone who’s never driven a race car just jump in and have fun? That’s what I hope, and that applies to me too. I’ve driven a lot of stuff in my life, but I’ve never driven a full downforce car, so my ultimate goal is just to drive this and have a good time. title: SEC v. Jarkesy: Two Years of Appellate Decisions - Legis1
content: Two years after the Supreme Court's landmark decision in SEC v. Jarkesy, a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report finds that federal agencies face mounting constitutional pressure over how they conduct enforcement proceedings. The Supreme Court held that the Seventh Amendment guarantees defendants a jury trial when the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities fraud. Justice Sotomayor noted in her dissent that Congress has enacted more than 200 statutes authorizing agencies to impose civil penalties. Following the Jarkesy ruling, the SEC could not use its own in-house Administrative Law Judges to adjudicate securities fraud cases. In Intuit, Inc. v. FTC, the Fifth Circuit held the FTC's in-house ALJ adjudication of deceptive advertising claims unconstitutional under Jarkesy. Similarly, the Fifth Circuit vacated a $57 million FCC forfeiture order against AT&T for customer location data privacy violations on April 17, 2025, finding that the FCC had acted as prosecutor, jury, and judge in violation of the Seventh Amendment. The CRS report surveys how federal appellate courts have interpreted, applied, extended, or limited Jarkesy across a wide range of federal agencies and enforcement contexts. The CRS report, published in August, examines the two-year legal and regulatory aftermath of the Supreme Court's June 2024 decision in SEC v. Jarkesy. Carriers who voluntarily paid the fines were found to have waived their jury trial right. The Communications Act, 47 U.S.C. § 504(a), allows carriers facing FCC fines to demand de novo district court review. The FCC has sought Supreme Court review of the AT&T decision. The Jarkesy decision has fundamentally disrupted federal enforcement across multiple agencies. While some courts have found narrow exceptions (such as when defendants voluntarily pay penalties), the broader trend is clear: agencies can no longer conduct civil penalty proceedings through in-house administrative judges without risking constitutional challenge. This shift forces agencies to either pursue cases in federal court (a slower, costlier process) or abandon enforcement actions altogether, as FERC has done with market manipulation cases. Congress is responding with legislation like the JUDGES Act (H.R. 1929) to restructure how administrative adjudication works, but the legal landscape remains unsettled. Pending cases, including a certiorari petition challenging whether legal restitution triggers jury trial rights, suggest the Supreme Court will continue refining Jarkesy's scope for years to come. title: Defend Community Integration Coalition Statement on Texas v. Kennedy Proposed Joint Resolution - aapd.com
content: Contact: Naomi Hess, communications@aapd.com; Jess Davidson, jdavidson@aapd.com The Defend Community Integration Coalition (DCIC) strongly condemns the recent proposed joint resolution filed August 31 in the ongoing case Texas v. Kennedy. The proposed resolution aims to strike down the 2024 community integration regulations under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. This action flies in the face of decades of judicial precedent and Congressional intent to ensure that community integration remains a civil right for all people with disabilities. As national disability rights leaders and allies, we have worked hard for decades to advance community integration as a foundational civil right for people with disabilities. We condemn any attacks aimed at undoing this work led by and for people with disabilities. For people with disabilities, there is no right more foundational than the right to make our own choices. Far too often, we find ourselves in the position where others decide our lives for us. It takes a lot to ensure that the choices we have are real choices. It has taken years to build the supports we need to go to school, work, eat, stay housed, and raise our children. As humans, we deserve the security of knowing that we have what we need to live our lives. Life is not just about getting three square meals a day and getting our meds on time. It is about growing, working, loving, dreaming, failing and reaching our potential. It is about deciding when to get up, when to go out, what to eat, and with whom to live. It is hard to do these things when we are forced to stay in congregate settings where we have no say over most aspects of our lives. Disabled people are survivors. We are spouses, parents, siblings, classmates, colleagues, and neighbors. Most of all, we are Americans determined to fight back against ideas and actions that take away our dignity and roll back years of hard-fought progress and rights. As a coalition we will continue to work together and fight for the full realization of the community integration mandate. Community integration of people with disabilities is non-negotiable. This is a monumental fight. In a moment like this, we need to join forces and work collectively. We are stronger together. Join the Defend Community Integration Coalition: https://bit.ly/3V8NfIy DCIC’s membership is comprised of Access Living, American Association of People with Disabilities, Autistic Self Advocacy Network, Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law, Caring Across Generations, Center for Public Representation, Disability Rights Education & Defense Fund, National Association of Councils on Developmental Disabilities, National Council on Independent Living, National Disability Rights Network, and United Spinal Association. Help the American Association of People with Disabilities increase the political and economic power of people with disabilities.

title: Verisk v. AccuLynx – Implications for Antitrust Approval - JD Supra
content:
On August 7, 2026, the Delaware Court of Chancery ordered Verisk Analytics, Inc. to move forward with its purportedly terminated $2.35 billion proposed acquisition of AccuLynx.com. The Court concluded that Verisk’s termination of the transaction was invalid and ordered specific performance. That remedy is extraordinary—and rarely ordered—in the M&A context, particularly where the parties must still substantially comply with a costly and time-consuming Second Request issued by the FTC and wait until expiration or termination of the applicable waiting period before they can close. Indeed, it has been nearly 18 years since Hexion v. Huntsman, the last significant “busted deal” litigation where a buyer was ordered to specifically perform its obligations to satisfy a regulatory approval covenant. Verisk is not the first busted deal litigation to arise out of a failure to satisfy antitrust-related closing conditions. But it differs in two important respects from other significant busted deal cases like In re Anthem-Cigna Merger Litigation, which concluded in 2020, and Albertsons v. Kroger, the ongoing dispute that followed successful state and federal challenges to the largest proposed supermarket merger in U.S. history. First, the antitrust risk in the Verisk/AccuLynx deal appeared quite low. Verisk and AccuLynx are not competitors, nor did they have an existing customer-supplier relationship. The parties addressed the antitrust risk in their contract accordingly. Second, the court did not find that Verisk acted in bad faith, failed to meet its regulatory efforts covenant, or otherwise attempted to scupper the deal. The Verisk decision, therefore, has significant implications for how parties apportion antitrust risk and provides a cautionary tale about best practices in engaging with the antitrust agencies. Verisk is a data analytics company offering claim assessment services to the insurance industry. Verisk refers to this as a “standard integration.” AccuLynx, by contrast, is a business and customer management software provider that serves roofing companies. Verisk and AccuLynx did not compete horizontally, nor did they have an existing customer-supplier relationship. But Verisk had worked with a handful of AccuLynx’s competitors, including ServiceTitan, Inc., to integrate with Verisk’s claims estimation products. While Verisk was pursuing its merger with AccuLynx, Verisk also was negotiating an “enhanced integration” with ServiceTitan. Unlike the standard integration, the enhanced integration would have enabled real-time pricing for claim estimation, but Verisk and ServiceTitan were far apart on commercial terms. Verisk and AccuLynx entered into a merger agreement, with terms reflecting the perceived lack of material antitrust risk. The agreement contemplated a four-month outside date, suitable for transactions likely to be subject to the standard 30-day Hart-Scott-Rodino waiting period and perhaps a 30-day extension following a pull and refile. The agreement also required only commercially reasonable efforts to obtain regulatory approvals. After the outside date, either party could terminate the agreement, provided its “willful conduct” had not been the “primary cause” for failing to satisfy regulatory closing conditions. Verisk decided to reserve any enhanced integration capabilities for AccuLynx. Six days after the deal signed, Verisk informed ServiceTitan that it would not move forward with the enhanced integration under negotiation because of the merger. Verisk instead entered into a standard integration with ServiceTitan. During its review, the FTC learned from ServiceTitan that Verisk had abandoned the enhanced integration as a result of the deal. The FTC formulated a novel “market reset” theory of harm, positing that Verisk would develop “a new, more sophisticated pricing integration” for AccuLynx and harm AccuLynx’s competitors by limiting them to the standard integration. FTC staff repeatedly asked Verisk whether it had abandoned any integrations because of the deal, and Verisk repeatedly responded it had not. Indeed, from Verisk’s perspective, it had not abandoned integration with ServiceTitan—it had merely changed what it was offering ServiceTitan. In October 2025, the FTC issued a Second Request. Verisk and AccuLynx executed a “quick look” timing agreement (i.e., prioritizing information that could help the agencies resolve their investigation without substantial compliance) to try to obtain expedited approval of the deal. The parties could not assuage the FTC’s concerns, and in late December—days before the outside date—the FTC informed the parties that they would need to fully comply with the Second Request. Having hit the outside date, Verisk delivered notice of termination and sought a declaratory judgment in the Court of Chancery that the termination was valid. AccuLynx in turn sought specific performance, arguing that Verisk was unable to invoke the termination clause because its “willful conduct” in terminating the enhanced integration discussions with ServiceTitan was the “primary cause” of the Second Request, which prevented the satisfaction of the regulatory closing conditions. Following trial and post-trial arguments in June and July 2026, the Court decided for AccuLynx. On August 18, 2026, Verisk appealed the decision. The upshot of the Court’s decision is that the parties lost over seven months in litigation and now must fully comply with the FTC’s Second Request and incur millions of dollars of additional costs and business distraction if they intend to close the deal. Alternatively, the Court’s decision gives AccuLynx leverage to negotiate a settlement with Verisk, whereby Verisk would effectively pay a reverse break fee in order to walk away from the deal. Verisk highlights the importance of involving antitrust counsel early in the deal process to carefully consider antitrust risk allocation and consider the impact on interactions with customers and suppliers, even for deals that appear low risk. Verisk appears to have originally had an independent reason to lose interest in an enhanced integration with ServiceTitan—they could not agree on how to price the new offering. But Verisk’s messaging to ServiceTitan solely referencing the AccuLynx deal as the reason for termination provided the FTC with a powerful piece of evidence for its novel theory of anticompetitive harm. The antitrust agencies routinely speak with interested stakeholders to assess whether a deal should be investigated and/or challenged. Changes to existing commercial relationships, or those being negotiated, may be reported to the reviewing agency. By involving antitrust counsel in these considerations, parties can appreciate how antitrust risk can evolve over the life of a deal. The case also offers a cautionary tale for careful drafting. Given the perceived low antitrust risk of the deal, Verisk negotiated to use only “commercially reasonable” efforts to secure regulatory approval. But it did not negotiate an explicit off-ramp if it were forced to substantially comply with a Second Request to get the deal done. While the Court did not conclude that the “commercially reasonable” standard required Second Request compliance, clarifying that Second Request compliance was not required could have resulted in a different outcome on specific performance. Verisk also could have negotiated a “willful breach” rather than “willful conduct” standard in order to preserve its termination right. Such terms may not have been palatable to AccuLynx absent other concessions (e.g., “hell or high water” efforts standard or a reverse break fee). While antitrust risk should not be the driving force in how the average deal is structured, parties should not assume a deal will sail through the antitrust agencies even if it is low-risk, and should instead think through how they might manage an extended antitrust review. As a final note, Verisk also touches on another topic of recent note: “quick look” review, which allows parties to respond to a narrower set of priority specifications within a Second Request that could resolve the agency’s investigation. The DOJ Antitrust Division recently announced a new model timing agreement that, among other things, formalizes the “quick look” approach (now called “Expedited Consideration”). Verisk shows that “quick look” review may not be very quick and could even have the practical effect of lengthening the antitrust review. The parties produced 400,000 documents from 16 custodians and engaged in close to 30 meetings with FTC staff over 64 days. Yet, the parties were unable to allay the FTC’s competitive concerns. Parties should think twice about relying solely on “quick look” (or “Expedited Consideration”) to get deals through without having a contingency plan in the event the reviewing agency requires full compliance with the Second Request. title: Carmelite Sisters for the Aged and Infirm v. Prince - Becket — Religious Liberty for All
content: For nearly 175 years, Catholic healthcare ministries have cared for the sick, the elderly, and the dying across Illinois. Guided by the belief that every life is a precious gift, these ministries accompany those nearing death with medical skill, prayer, and love until God calls them home. But now Illinois is threatening them with significant fines and penalties unless they help patients obtain lethal suicide drugs—forcing Catholic hospitals, religious sisters, and healthcare professionals to violate their faith or abandon the very people they serve. For millennia, Catholics around the world have operated healthcare ministries to serve the sick and dying. Rooted in Christ’s command to care for the “least of these,” these ministries put their faith into practice by offering excellent medical care, spiritual support, sacramental care, and end-of-life accompaniment to the most vulnerable. Even when a patient is facing a terminal illness and cannot be cured, Catholic providers give their all to surround them with the greatest love imaginable, to alleviate their suffering, and to ignite in them a hope for the world to come. Illinois has long benefited from this compassionate service. For nearly 175 years, Catholic healthcare ministries have been a refuge for the sick, elderly, and dying across Illinois.  Today, that work includes Catholic hospitals treating millions of patients each year. It also includes the work of religious Sisters caring for the elderly, and faithful Catholic laypeople serving as healthcare professionals in every part of the state. Since 1964, the Carmelite Sisters for the Aged and Infirm have cared for elderly Illinoisans at St. Patrick’s Residence in Naperville, providing long-term, rehabilitative, and palliative care alongside daily prayer and loving presence—ensuring that no resident dies alone. The Little Sisters of the Poor first came to Illinois in 1876 to minister to those devastated by the Great Chicago Fire. Today, they continue caring for the elderly in Chicago and Palatine, where they accompany those they serve in a spirit of hospitality, companionship, and trust in God’s providence. That same commitment to healing has guided Luke Vander Bleek throughout his career as a pharmacist. For the past forty years, he has sought to use his pharmaceutical skills to serve and heal his community, all motivated by his Catholic faith. He currently runs a community pharmacy in Morrison, Illinois, a town of 4,000 two hours west of Chicago. Illinois tries to strong-arm nuns into its regime of death In 2026, Illinois passed its End-of-Life Options for Terminally Ill Patients Act (EOLOA), allowing terminally ill adults to obtain lethal drugs to end their lives. Yet the law does not merely permit assisted suicide: it forces objecting healthcare providers into its machinery. Religious providers who object to participating in assisted suicide must still inform patients about their “right” to kill themselves, help them qualify for lethal drugs, and pass them along to someone willing to help them obtain those drugs. Meanwhile, pharmacists like Vander Bleek must fill lethal prescriptions or refer patients to another pharmacy that will. In other words, Illinois makes religious healthcare providers punch the patient’s ticket to death even when doing so violates their faith. Illinois also imposes a gag order on religious caregivers who want to speak a life-affirming message against suicide. EOLOA’s definition of coercion and undue influence is so broad that it risks punishing the Sisters and healthcare providers in the Archdiocese simply for telling a suffering patient, “Don’t kill yourself. Jesus loves you. Your life is precious.” Catholic teaching forbids the Archdiocese’s healthcare ministries, the Sisters, and Vander Bleek from prescribing life-ending drugs, directing patients to obtain them, or helping facilitate a patient’s suicide in any way.  The Church teaches that when a person is suffering deeply, the proper response is loving accompaniment—not abandonment to death.Rather, they accept death as the natural end to a life well-lived: to accept it as it comes, neither artificially hastening it through any means, nor artificially prolonging it through burdensome technological and medical advancements that provide no reasonable benefit. Catholic ministries fight for their freedom to care With Becket’s help, Cardinal Cupich, the Carmelite Sisters, the Little Sisters, and Vander Bleek filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block Illinois’ assisted-suicide law before it takes effect on September 12, 2026. The lawsuit asks the court to protect their freedom to continue caring for the sick, elderly, and dying in accordance with their Catholic faith. The lawsuit also seeks to protect the rights of patients who want the freedom to choose care providers who will not offer them suicide. Illinois’ actions violate core constitutional protections for religious freedom and freedom of speech. The government cannot force Catholic ministries and healthcare professionals to violate their faith by helping patients obtain suicide pills. Nor can it gag Catholic doctors, nurses, caregivers, and pharmacists from offering life-affirming counsel and force them instead to deliver the state’s preferred message about suicide. Federal law further protects these providers by banning the use of federal health care funds for assisted suicide and by forbidding Illinois from discriminating against those who, like Becket’s clients, refuse to participate in assisted suicide. For generations, Catholic healthcare ministries have offered the sick and dying across Illinois a place of peace, prayer, and love at the end of life. Illinois should stop trampling religious freedom and forcing its message of death on vulnerable patients. Subscribe to receive our monthly newsletter and breaking news updates.

title: Grimes 'Hazily' Recalls Writing the Song 'Witch v Witch' With Charli xcx - Billboard
content:
A purported recording of the never-released song posted by a fan sounds like a dark robot hyperpop track with ethereal vocals from Charli. Add “Witch v Witch” to the great pile of never-released songs from Charli xcx. In a back-and-forth with Grimes over the past 24 hours, the “360” singer vaguely recalled recording the song with Grimes years ago, though neither artist seems to be able to place exactly when, where or how it came together. The whole conversation began when a fan posted a purported version of the dark track sourced from a YouTube video of unclear provenance on X on Tuesday (Sept. 1), revealing a spare, jackhammer beat hyperpop dance tune in which the chorus is repeated in a robotic, distorted voice while a voice that sounds a lot like Charli’s sings, “Don’t ever lean on me/ Get closer, you hold me/ Secrets you told me.” “coming across a random unreleased charli scrap and it being the best song of all time is lowkey way too common god she is such a talent,” wrote the fan who posted the clip. Charli responded quickly, writing “i could be wrong but i thinkkkkkk this is me and grimes.” A few hours later, Grimes weighed in, responding, “I very hazily remember writing ‘witch v witch’ but I can’t conjure the session in my mind – but I remember making the art- I remember ‘witch v witch’ haha – I know we did this I just can’t recall where or when. i feel like I did a meh initial production and I feel like someone has taken another pass over the prod and made it better here maybe AG.” The latter appears to be a reference to British producer and frequent Grimes collaborator A.G. Cook., who executive produced xcx’s 2019 album Charli and also worked on several tracks from her 2020 How I’m Feeling Now LP, as well as 2022’s Crash and her massive 2024 breakthrough, brat. At press time spokespeople for both artists had not returned Billboard‘s request for comment. Once Grimes weighed in, Charli responded, “yessss you’re right. i think ag worked on this at a later point. we worked at your place one night in la quite a long time ago i think. i like it too!” Grimes teased her sixth studio album, Psy Opera, in April of this year, with no release date announced so far. A collaboration with virtual singer Hatsune Miku called “Miku-Maxxing” was released last month as the lead single from the upcoming EP Beyond Borders Vol. 1: Emerge Mode Miku. Charli appeared in a series of films this year, including the tour mockumentary The Moment, Gregg Araki’s I Want Your Sex, the comedy The Gallerist and the horror remake Faces of Death. She released her eighth studio album, the Cook co-produced Music, Fashion, Film, in July. Your email address will not be published.

title: Great Britain’s Wild, Dodge Viper V-10-Powered Sports Car From the Aughts Is Coming Back - Road & Track
content: The revived British brand building a handful of cars to original spec from unused chassis. After a few misfired attempts at coming back since its market departure 15 years ago, Bristol Cars has announced a triumphant return just in time for its 80th anniversary. Instead of using that milestone as an opportunity to look forward, the company is throwing it back to the Aughts with a limited run of new Bristol Fighter supercars announced at Salon Privé. The Bristol Fighter was initially introduced in 2004, and would ultimately serve as the brand’s last production car completed before the company’s liquidation in 2011. (There have been attempts to push new sheetmetal out in the intervening years, but circumstances have not been favorable to the painfully low-volume brand.) That said, the Fighter itself was a fitting tribute to the brand’s origins in wartime aircraft production, bringing some seriously modern performance for the time to market. Its box-section chassis with bodywork developed by Brabham Formula One’s Max Boxstrom was a solid start, but the real magic of the Fighter came under the hand-beaten panels. Pulling a reverse Carroll Shelby, Bristol sourced 8.0-liter V-10 engines from Dodge to power the cars. The Fighters were initially offered in 525-horsepower specification, but later Fighter S models saw that figure jump closer to 600 hp. The automaker claims that was enough shove to make the Fighter soar to 210 mph. Those are figures the new car aims to match. Despite its intriguing styling and undeniable Detroit-sourced grunt, the Fighter never quite took off. The brand is thought to have sold just 15 or so cars before the end of the run. That said, five leftover chassis remained, and those will serve as the basis for this new run of cars. The revived brand says that it plans to build these cars back to original spec, and that they will be working with a British manufacturing partner to help complete the builds. Customers will essentially have free range to make the cars as they see fit, including the ability to select a left-hand drive configuration. This first build is more traditional in its approach, however, going for right-hand drive and a timeless black-over-tan color scheme. “Bringing Bristol Cars back is about far more than reviving a name; it is about bringing back the spirit of a marque that has always stood apart. Bristol has a remarkable story, from its roots in aviation and engineering to the extraordinary and exclusive cars it crafted,” said Paul King, director of Bristol Cars. “We have brought together an exceptional combination of heritage, knowledge, engineering and craftsmanship. This is the beginning of Bristol’s return, and there is much more to come.” It’s safe to assume that each of the four remaining Bristol Fighter builds are going to be tremendously expensive, as the automaker will not publicly share pricing information. That said, this is a unique opportunity for a die-hard group of fans to get their hands on a genuine Fighter. That’s gotta be at least a little bit cooler than your typical restomod project. He may daily drive an aging Mustang, but his Porsche 944 and NB Miata both take up most of his free time. We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we back.

title: Fraser Industries CEO Patrick V. Kelly on shipbuilding growth, modernization - WorkBoat
content: You may unsubscribe from our mailing list at any time. Diversified Communications | 121 Free Street, Portland, ME 04101 | +1 207-842-5500 BREAKING NEWS: The WorkBoat Show returns to New Orleans, Dec. 2-4. Registration is now open. Get your free pass today → Fraser Industries CEO Patrick V. Kelly sees modernization, workforce development, and greater use of Great Lakes shipbuilding capacity as keys to the company’s next phase of growth. Fraser Industries photo. WorkBoat sat down with Patrick V. Kelly, CEO of Fraser Industries LLC, to discuss how the 138-year-old Superior, Wis., shipyard is positioning itself for growth as the United States looks to expand domestic shipbuilding capacity. WorkBoat sat down with Patrick V. Kelly, CEO of Fraser Industries LLC, to discuss how the 138-year-old Superior, Wis., shipyard is positioning itself for growth as the United States looks to expand domestic shipbuilding capacity. Kelly discusses Fraser’s recent shipyard modernization memorandum of understanding with HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, the Great Lakes Alliance of Shipyards’ pursuit of the Coast Guard’s Homeland Security Cutter-Light program, workforce development, and the role the Great Lakes could play in a broader maritime resurgence. Fraser is a very diversified shipyard. We repair lakers, including vessels up to 1,000 feet long, and build new vessels for commercial and military customers. We work in aluminum and steel. The combination of repair and new construction makes us a pretty unique shipyard. Our location in the Duluth [Minn.]-Superior [Wis.] Harbor complex, a top 20 North American port by tonnage, makes us a great location for repair work. Lakers come in and out almost by the hour, moving taconite, grain, coal, other commodity products, and wind turbine components, to name a few. That leads to work from long-term customers as well as vessels moving through the harbor that need repairs. We are busiest in January, February, and March, when the Great Lakes ships come off the water because of winter ice and weather. We are like an Indianapolis pit crew. Year-round, we employ about 200 people, but we ramp up to 600 people during the winter months. Outside of that season, I do not have enough repair work to keep all of those people working. We are trying to fill that gap with new construction through Lake Assault Boats, Northern Engineering, and Fraser Shipyards. The strongest demand, I believe, comes from the movement of taconite for steel manufacturing. As the United States ramps up its industrial base, steel manufacturing becomes critically important, and more iron ore will move from the Duluth-Superior Harbor complex to mills throughout the Great Lakes. That is just the beginning. As we talk about reindustrializing North America, the Great Lakes is a fabulous place to do business. The Great Lakes system, the St. Lawrence Seaway, maritime operators, ports, and terminals are all roughly 50% utilized. We are significantly underutilized, which makes the region an ideal place to bring new business and new ways of doing business. The Great Lakes is open and ready to go. If you compare U.S. shipbuilders with our Korean counterparts, we have a lot to learn. Fraser is a terrific shipyard. We have operated continuously for 138 years, and you do not set that kind of longevity record by doing things poorly. However, we recognize that we have a lot to learn, and we are working to leapfrog existing shipbuilding technologies and bring the best available technology into the yard. Larger coastal yards are receiving major contracts, developing extended backlogs, and taking longer to turn vessels around. That creates opportunities for smaller yards like Fraser to take on larger projects. We doubled our output of vessels delivered from 2023 to 2026, and we are working to double it again in 2027 and 2028. We currently use about 15 acres of the 100 acres we own, so we can add significant production capacity. We also have a strong workforce, inexpensive electricity, and readily available natural gas. HD Hyundai sees the same opportunity to bring a shipyard of the future to the Great Lakes for additional commercial and military work. We are extremely excited about the Great Lakes Alliance of Shipyards. Our government could not be clearer. This is about delivering boats, vessels, and ships, and accelerating the timeline to delivery. Three yards working together can deliver vessels faster than one shipyard can on its own. We are initially focused on the Coast Guard’s Homeland Security Cutter-Light program. These are icebreaking tugboats about 65 or 70 feet long, and the Coast Guard is looking for seven vessels under the full contract. We believe we can deliver all seven in about one-third the time it would take an individual shipyard. We hope that gets noticed by the Coast Guard and that we are the winning group. It would bring more work to the Great Lakes and make all three yards better for the next opportunity. It is all about the pace of delivery. Each shipyard would build complete vessels. We will share the design and engineering work, and much of the procurement will be handled centrally. We will do everything possible to standardize the process and will make certain that each shipyard is building the same vessel for the Coast Guard. Our goal is that you would not be able to tell which yard built which vessel, other than the stamp and nameplate. We are ruthlessly standardizing to meet the Coast Guard’s requirements. Most shipyards are constrained by acreage. Communities have grown around them, and they have fully utilized the land available. Coastal shipyards are also constrained by workforce, with many other industries competing for people. Fraser does not have those same constraints. We have space to expand in Superior, and we have a great workforce. We could hire more people if we had the opportunity to put them to work. I will not say it is easy to find a skilled or trained workforce, but there are great people in the technical and community college programs around us. We support six different colleges and programs with surplus equipment that is still good for training, scrap steel and aluminum, and employees who teach classes after their shifts. We support those programs and hire their graduates. In some cases, we are hiring 80% of a graduating class. With additional funding, those programs tell us they could accept more students. As more work comes to the yard, we can hire more people and invest through grants and other support in the training programs around us. It becomes a virtuous loop. HD Hyundai sees the same opportunity. In Superior, it would mean better utilizing our 100-acre campus, completing expansion projects, adding production space, increasing employment, and bringing new technologies into the yard. We also see opportunities to expand shipbuilding and repair elsewhere around the Great Lakes. Other locations make sense, including Lake Erie, Lake Ontario, and the St. Lawrence Seaway. We would like to participate in those expansions and buildouts. The Great Lakes have unique geographic advantages. Lake Michigan is the only large body of water surrounded completely by U.S. states, making it an ideal test bed for airborne, surface, and subsurface drone arrays where outside parties could not listen in or gain access. It is a bit like Area 51 for the Air Force. Some people already refer to Lake Michigan as Area 52. The Great Lakes provide deepwater, ocean-like conditions, severe sea states, and winter ice. As Arctic work becomes more important, learning to operate in and under ice will become increasingly valuable. There are all sorts of maritime opportunities to do more on the Great Lakes.
