title: The Art of Research: “Chandra” V. Chandrasekar - Colorado State University News
content: Walter Scott, Jr. College of EngineeringDepartment of Electrical and Computer Engineering Interviewed by Josh RhotenPhotos by Matthew StaverPublished Sept. 3, 2026 Editor’s note: The Art of Research is a series focused on in-depth conversations with University Distinguished Professors about their work and careers. Chandra V. Chandrasekar started his illustrious career as a radar scientist by flying into storms to take photographs of raindrops. He wanted to understand their exact shape – not teardrops, as it turns out, but little spherical blobs. That mattered, Chandra and his graduate adviser realized, because understanding the shape of raindrops could lead to development of radar systems that would deliver more precise data about storm severity. This information, in turn, would come to underpin modern weather forecasting aimed at saving lives and property – the motivation that drives Chandra’s work. Many of these advancements have occurred at CSU with Chandra’s leadership. “Water is a primary element of life – water controls our lives,” said the scientist known as Chandra to friends, colleagues and students alike. “So, lack of water is a problem. Too much water is a problem. The first step to dealing with that problem is to measure precipitation very accurately. Once we know how much water is coming in, we can manage it better.” With that goal in mind, Chandra has become an international leader in creating and using radar systems to better forecast severe weather and to study the Earth’s climate. After growing up and attending a university in India, Chandra earned master’s and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering at Colorado State University in the 1980s. With research straddling the fields of electrical engineering and atmospheric science, he is now a University Distinguished Professor recognized for his high-impact accomplishments by numerous groups around the world. In fact, he may be one of few people in the world who can claim simultaneous election as a fellow of multiple engineering and science societies, including the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, International Union of Radio Science, American Meteorological Society, American Geophysical Union and the National Academy of Inventors. And even that list, as impressive as it is, is not fully representative of the breadth of his achievements. He has also served as a distinguished visiting researcher with the National Research Council of Italy and the NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; not to mention being knighted in Finland for his work with Finnish Meteorological Institute and University of Helsinki, where he worked to commercialize technologies for broader adoption. His research has been cited in over 300 articles, and he is the author of multiple books on topics including the development of dual-polarization radar, which he helped pioneer at CSU. It is the industry standard today. Meanwhile, his resume also includes past leadership roles in many large multi-agency, national level experiments involving many different radars, aircraft and ground instrumentation. He is also the director of the CSU-CHILL radar facility near Greeley, where he plays an important role in maintaining it as one of the most advanced meteorological radar systems in the world. The radar facility is a crown jewel of CSU’s research infrastructure, and many graduate and undergraduate students get hands-on experience there. It’s just the latest example of his research work in action. CSU’s SOURCE sat down with Chandra to hear more about his research accomplishments, his thoughts on the challenges of conducting interdisciplinary research and his path to Colorado State University. Tell me about your path to CSU? How did you arrive here after getting your undergraduate degree in India? Well, I did my undergraduate in India from a famous school: the Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur. I was working on a technology called near field scanning at that point. It is a measurement technique that maps electromagnetic fields close to an antenna or radar. That technology was really needed to first test and then build the current remote-sensing systems we have today. There was a big race going on internationally to develop these systems, so I was sort of at the heart of that. I was recruited to CSU because of my knowledge in that field and was a part of the research with assignments at the National Center for Atmospheric Research and the National Bureau of Standards which eventually became the National Institute of Standards and Technology. At the same time, I got a graduate degree and eventually my Ph.D. in 1986 from CSU and have been at here pretty much ever since. Aside from a stint at the University of Alabama, Huntsville with NASA Marshall Space Flight Center which was, of course, interested in radar development at that point as well. I came back to CSU in 1990 to lead work within the CSU-CHILL National Weather Radar Facility, which is still a top facility in the world today. Why did you focus on radars? Why was that a topic you originally started to research? It’s important to understand first that radar is a hand-me-down technology from the military. It was originally designed to see where aircraft were but has now, obviously, become common for weather prediction and forecasting. The original radars were not built for seeing into storms. They were built to see airplanes. So, there were some inherent challenges in making them useful for weather prediction. Planes are big and solid where drops are soft and in large groups, for a start. Somewhere along the line, I got in with my then adviser who was studying the actual shape of raindrops for this reason. We wanted to know the exact composition of storms so we could better interpret the signals that were bouncing back off them and returning to us. I was an electrical engineer who built and worked with these systems. But we eventually came to realize that if we understood the actual shape of the rain drops, we could build the radar to better understand the contents of a storm. So literally, I’m not even joking, I actually flew on airplanes and as a young researcher to take pictures of raindrops. With that we discovered that raindrops are not tear-shaped as most people assume. They are shaped more round like M&Ms candy. You can imagine how an audience of atmospheric researchers reacted to a young electrical engineer telling them this, but I tried to be diligent and explain how that changes the signals we are looking for to determine the content of these storms. I wound up as an author on some of the earliest papers talking about the shape of drops and how it impacts radar functions. This was well before the days of interdisciplinary research being cool and these were published in atmospheric science journals. It is still one of my most widely cited papers. But anyway, fast forward. Using those principles, we developed a new class of radars called dual polarization – or polarimetric radars. Traditional radars send a single pulse of energy and measure how much of that energy came back after bouncing off something it is targeting. The new systems we developed here at CSU transmit and receive pulses in both a horizontal and vertical orientation at the same time. Rain drops – or anything else inside these storms like hail, snowflakes or debris – change the signal sent back in different and specific ways based on their shape. We can tell a lot more about the makeup of these storms by processing and comparing returns from these signals, which is an electrical engineering question at its core. I think I am reducing your thoughts on this down quite a bit in this section and the next. If there is anything more to add about the value of dual-polar or how it works please feel free to add? You have written a book or two on the subject of dual-polarization now? That is right. With traditional radars the signal hits an object and comes back. In the old days you just knew there was a blob of a storm or something there. You didn’t know if it had rain or ice or snow. You could tell from the turnaround return time how far away it was and maybe how big overall. We realized that you needed to be able to see these type of drops so you knew for sure it was rain. To do that, we sent signals in what is called two polarizations – that just describes the way the wave’s energy oscillates in space. One is horizontal polarization and another one is vertical polarization. Very simple. It’s like, so simple that like a lot of people will go, Why didn’t I think of that? I do remember the days when everybody said dual polarization wouldn’t work, but today you can’t buy a non-dual polarization radar. That’s the only thing the market makes. It’s one of the reasons I tell young people to stick with an idea even if others are telling them it will never work. Being able to better say what the composition of a storm is helps with forecasting and letting people know what to expect, right? Dual-polarization is like doing a CAT scan inside your body at a hospital. The radar signal goes inside the storm and tells us exactly what is in there. You can immediately tell if it’s just another afternoon storm or if it’s a big one with hail at the core. From there you can watch it move and start to make predictions about that. It can also clearly tell you the amount of water that’s in the storms, which is important for flooding. And it can also very clearly distinguish between water and ice. In the old days, you had to send a weather balloon to do that, which had its own challenges and limitations. It was a huge deal and now it’s taken for granted. The technology I am describing was pretty much developed here at CSU and is now the gold standard around the world. I want to be careful to say I’m not the smartest guy; I just happened to be at the right place at the right time when this was all going on. There was a lot of interest, and these systems became the workhorse of the National Weather Service as we see it today. I spent my next 30 years touring and lecturing around the world about how to build and use them. And then we wrote the first book on that 20 years ago. The interesting thing is: When you are the first guy doing something, all the symbols you make for equations and things for the first time? They become permanent symbols in the field. So now, I see all of these that were developed so long ago still looking back at me across the research. I have that kind of luck, I guess. That is incredible to see your impact over time in that way though. I understand you also pioneered linking different radars together to give a fuller picture across a region? Yes, that is another part of the engineering side of my work. It goes back to a colleague of mine driving home from Greeley, where we had and still have our CHILL radar systems set up. It was snowing and a combine-tractor was coming, so he tried to move off the road and basically wound up in a ditch. He had to spend the night in the car and – he was a sturdy guy – but I said, ‘Look this cannot happen, we should be able to access these systems remotely.’ That was how we got started making these radars function and communicate over the internet. Today this is automatic, but it took a lot of engineering to make happen. Is that part of your work with the Engineering Research Center for Collaborative Adaptive Sensing of the Atmosphere? Yes, a lot of great research and work came out of that collaboration that I am proud of. It came out of a spontaneous partnership that started around in 2003 and ran for more than 10 years. At that point there were many different types of large radar systems in operation depending on where you were in the world. S-Band in China and India and C-Band in Europe, for example that could ‘see’ further out but with less detail. These also took a lot of resources to initially build and set up. It essentially needs large government investment to get these systems going and then you couldn’t move them if needed. So they were limited in a few ways. National Science Foundation Engineering Research Centers are huge, interdisciplinary research projects that span multiple universities, industry, and agencies. They have tens of millions of dollars in funding from the National Science Foundation over the course of several years to study large problems that require many different types of expertise. Our center – where I was essentially the chief technical officer – was launched to try and develop ways to miniaturize these radar systems and then pioneer distributed collaborative adaptive sensing through the resulting network. That approach uses dense networks of small, low-power, X-band dual-polarization radars that are controlled directly by forecasters. The goal was to put these smaller, high-frequency systems that can ‘see’ better over short distances now where more people actually live to better follow potentially dangerous storms better. They provide better resolution and are not limited like some of the larger traditional radar systems. But, well, let me put it this way: It is not a piece of cake just to build a small radar that operates at higher frequencies. Otherwise, people would have done it a long time ago! There was a lot of physics-based limitations that had to be overcome and we did that work through the center. Today that work has been commercialized and is very common. Where has artificial intelligence come into your research? How will that change our ability to predict and warn about destructive storms with the systems and technology you are describing? With the center, we were starting to connect radars together through the internet. Now we are connecting them to the AI. It’s a perfect match because the field and technology develop so much data, which is what these AI systems hunger for. We have data flowing like it was coming out of fire hydrants, and we really did not even know what to do with in some ways before now getting access to these large computing systems that can handle and make sense of them. I will give you an example. Right now, I am working on a project with NVIDIA that highlights this change with predicting damaging hail. We are the leading research institution for it with partners at CSU from the Departments of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Atmospheric Science, and the Cooperative Institute for Research in the Atmosphere. This has connections to the National Science Foundation funded ASCEND Engine in Colorado and Wyoming as well. Hail can be very destructive in our northern Colorado and Wyoming region, and an obvious goal would be to increase warning times ahead of it. However, we still don’t fully understand which way these storms may move and where new cells can form. That relates to a storm’s strengthening process towards those more damaging scenarios. At this point, we can forecast what will happen in perhaps the next 30 to 40 minutes. For this project we trained a specialized version of the NVIDIA Earth-2 StormScope Nowcasting model using data from a collection of the radar systems we operate at CSU. The AI system can take all of that information from different systems and locations in and then generate a better prediction much faster than current processes. The resulting models also capture storm evolution and intensity very well and can give maybe two hours of warning time instead. That is a huge improvement! There was a point where I was telling everyone that AI would change how all of this worked and was essentially laughed out of the room. But I published on the topic at the time and now it has come back around. In those days we didn’t have enough computing power to make these models. Now we can assimilate more data and do it better. That makes a big difference in operationalizing this stuff. You have been cited in many publications across engineering and the atmospheric sciences. What are your thoughts on being part of both communities and doing interdisciplinary work every day? I started doing interdisciplinary work before it was cool. Or maybe you could say I was doing it when it was still, sort of, not popular. I was involved in cool results from the field of atmospheric science, but electrical engineers didn’t really appreciate that. Over time I had to push to publish in essentially two different fields. Which side of the house kind of accepted you more? It sounds more like atmospheric colleagues saw the value early on? No, it’s not like that. Everyone will accept results, but the systems in academia can create silos. If you are going for tenure in one area you publish in one set of journals. For another, there is another venue for your papers. One positive net result though is that I am a fellow of both Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers and the American Meteorological Society as well as the American Geophysical Union. Another positive is that my team can work on both sides of a project in house. The left half of me is an atmospheric scientist and the right half is an engineer. That’s a big advantage. You don’t have to go find a waffle maker, as it were. You are the waffle maker, and you also have the ice cream. You are also a fellow of many other organizations, including the National Academy of Inventors. I understand that you have, potentially, the most patents of anyone affiliated with CSU? Is that true and what are your feelings about entrepreneurship? I am not sure I have the most patents, but I have many licensed patents. Either way, I think licensing is one of the most effective ways to have technology developed in academia reach people in the real world. And I do think that there is a connection between this type entrepreneurial work and our university’s land-grant mission. A large part of that mission is developing new technologies and opportunities as well as the workforce needed to use them. It is not just about curiosity-driven research – all though of course there is always that aspect. It’s instead more of a focus on practical work that can be put into use – in our case, to save lives. The research center I was mentioning is a great example of all of this. We were required to publish in high-end journals of course, but that alone is not sufficient for impact. The goal was also to produce and help integrate new technology. Other universities in that project were also land-grant institutions, so there was a similar goal across much of the shared work. The legacy still lives on today in that way. The center only ran for about 10 years, but I am still involved in projects such as one in the San Francisco and Bay Area that can trace their origin to the work we pioneered there. With that project, we are combining observations and models to improve monitoring and forecasts of precipitation, streamflow, and coastal flooding in complex terrain. One positive net result though is that I am a fellow of both Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers and the American Meteorological Society as well as the American Geophysical Union. Another positive is that my team can work on both sides of a project in house. The left half of me is an atmospheric scientist and the right half is an engineer. That’s a big advantage. You don’t have to go find a waffle maker, as it were. You are the waffle maker, and you also have the ice cream. What else are you working on today that excites you? I have been working with students to develop small satellites that can carry radar systems into space. CSU has a long history with these types of remote sensing projects including TEMPEST-D and the soon-to-launch INCUS mission – both of which I am involved in. But here I am talking about very small vehicles that give students a chance to build the system and eventually deploy it for themselves in pursuit of the same types of questions. And then, obviously, we are still working with the CSU-CHILL Radar system near Greeley. The radar is an advanced, dual-polarized dual-wavelength weather radar system. I can go into the details about the system, but we are still doing research to advance developments in radar meteorology, radio frequency engineering and remote sensing. It is a very advanced research instrument and gives students a unique opportunity to gain hands-on experience with applied signal processing and atmospheric analytics. title: QJMotor patents 'V-twin single' engine with dummy piston balancer in the US - Motorcycle News
content:
The parent company of Chinese bike firm QJMotor have filed a US patent for their ‘V-twin single’ engine design, which uses a dummy second piston as a balancer. The engine has a single crankcase with two cylinder bores drilled into it, arranged in an 80-degree V-shape – visually resembling a normal V-twin. But only one of those two bores is a genuine combustion cylinder; the other is a ‘balancing cylinder’ that never ignites fuel or produces power. On the combustion side, the real cylinder contains a standard piston that does the actual work: intake, compression, combustion, exhaust – driving the crankshaft in the normal way. The dummy cylinder on the other side contains a second piston connected to the same crankshaft via a second connecting rod. The second piston has a through air vent – essentially a hole running from its top face to its bottom face. Because of this vent, the piston can move up and down inside its bore without ever compressing or pumping air. It does no thermodynamic work at all; it simply moves as a counterweight, driven purely by the crankshaft’s rotation, to physically cancel out the vibration produced by the real piston’s motion. This second piston also has no piston rings around it, unlike a normal piston, since it isn’t sealing a combustion chamber – it just needs to be guided smoothly up and down. Removing the rings cuts friction and drag, which the patent identifies as the main flaw in older attempts at this idea. Both connecting rods share the same crankpin, keeping the whole assembly compact. Despite the engine casing itself being set at 80 degrees, the pistons are set at up to 90 degrees, to optimise the balancing effect the dummy creates. See the red and blue lines below. This has been achieved by housing the second cylinder in a separate insert – called the connecting base – that bolts onto the crankcase via a flange. This is possible because the balancing cylinder’s outer diameter is smaller than the narrowest point of the bore it sits in, rather than being a tight, sealed fit. That gives the second piston enough travel to do its balancing job properly despite its offset line of travel. So, rather than simply following the geometry of the original block, the balancing cylinder can be tilted away, opening up the effective angle between the two cylinders’ axes. The connecting base also has cooling ribs around its outside, to stop heat building up inside the non-combusting cylinder, since it doesn’t get the cooling benefit of intake and exhaust airflow that a normal cylinder would. The stated goal is to give a single-cylinder engine the smoothness of a proper balance-shaft system, but at lower manufacturing cost and complexity. It’s cheaper and less complicated because it relies on existing crankcase tooling and architecture already set up for a V-twin-style multi-cylinder casting, rather than adding a separate geared balance shaft assembly. The patent explicitly frames this as a way to control production costs on small-displacement engines while still meeting modern requirements for reduced vibration. Yes, sort of. QJMotor’s design is conceptually similar to the approach Ducati’s Massimo Bordi first tried, and later abandoned, during early development of the 1993 Supermono. Bordi’s original prototype used the same principle – a dummy piston acting purely as a balancer – before the drag it created forced him to switch to a double-conrod ‘doppia bielletta’ solution for the production bike. The patent doesn’t name a specific host engine or state a capacity anywhere in the document. However, the 80-degree V-angle described matches the layout of Qianjiang’s existing 997cc Morbidelli/MBP V-twin. Certainly, a smooth and cheap to produce 500cc single with around 40bhp would be an attractive prospect for a high-revving, cost-conscious single-cylinder platform aimed at the A2 market. The US publication of the design is the latest step in a patent timeline stretching back to August 2022, when the firm first filed an application for the engine in China. The following year, QJMotor filed a PCT application – a mechanism that allows for the simultaneous pursuit of patent protection across around 150 member countries. This latest US document was then filed last year, before being published by the United States Patent and Trademark Office on August 27, 2026. Rather than a forgotten or abandoned filing, it could be that Qianjiang has been securing legal ownership of the design specifically with the US market in mind. Whether this design ever reaches a production Benelli or QJMotor model remains to be seen. But three decades on from Bordi’s abandoned prototype, it’s a reminder that some of the cleverest ideas in engine design have a habit of resurfacing. title: Toyota's Major RAV4 Fumble Will Be The Honda CR-V's Greatest Victory - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update We look at how dealer markups early on in the year may have affected RAV4 sales both in the short and long term. The Toyota RAV4 was about to mark 10 years in a row as the best-selling "not a pickup" in the United States. A botched product launch affected sales in a big way early this year, and as we progress through 2026, there are signs of a recovery. But they're small signs, and that's not good when your main competitor is charging up the sales charts like crazy. At this point, Toyota will need a run of record-setting months if the company wants to catch the Honda CR-V this year. Last month, Toyota dealers across the US moved 34,232 units of the ever-popular RAV4 crossover. For any other automaker, that would be a smash hit. For Toyota, it's a big disappointment, though it's still an improvement in the grand scheme. That figure represents a sales drop of 19% over August 2025, but it's better than Toyota's year-to-date sales total, which is down 32% over the first eight months of 2025. It's way better than in February, when RAV4 sales dropped 57% from the same month last year, selling just 16,098. At one point, it looked ready to lose to Tacoma, Corolla, and Camry on Toyota's own charts. At this point, it's still behind the hot-selling Camry sedan. With Toyota down to eighth place or so on the charts for 2026 (not every automaker reports every month), Honda is enjoying its time in the sun. Sales of the CR-V were up 10% in August year-over-year, with 37,607 units leaving dealers. The CR-V is up 8.3% on the year, and has moved 302,056 vehicles. That puts Honda on pace for around 443,000 CR-Vs this year, a figure that will likely make it the top-selling not-a-truck. The Ford F-Series and Chevrolet Silverado lines will likely keep their traditional first and second-place overall. To be blunt, catching the Honda CR-V at this point is highly unlikely. Anything is possible, but don't hold your breath. Here's why. The RAV4 is currently 82,584 units behind the CR-V, with four months remaining in the year. Toyota would need to sell 20,000 units more than Honda every month for the rest of the year to catch it. The best month ever for RAV4 was in March 2021, when Toyota sold just over 47,000. If it could match that pace each month, then sell an additional 10,000 every month, it could just about tie with Honda. Or CR-V sales could crater, but that seems extremely unlikely. Then again, so did Toyota's current position. As for what went wrong? Well... Toyota stopped building RAV4s at the company's largest plant in the world. Turns out, that makes a difference. When Toyota made the change to the latest generation of RAV4, it phased in the change over the multiple factories that build it. That's common, and it's normal to see a dip for a month or two during the change. Toyota changed over plants in Japan and Canada first. They built more RAV4s for the US market, so it made sense. But its Kentucky plant, which builds roughly 6,700 units per month, wasn't building the SUV for months. That figure doesn't add up to the total drop, but when you combine it with missed weeks at the other two plants, you get the deficit. The automaker hasn't explained why it took until June to start building the 2026 RAV4, when it started in Japan before the end of 2025 and Canada in January. Queries earlier this summer were met with non-answers. But hey, better late than never. Reduced production was of course the main stumbling block for Toyota, not allowing the automaker to supply in great enough quantities to match demand. Some dealers decided to try and capitalize on this, and began adding significant markups to even base grades of the all-new RAV4 earlier in the year. We've covered these RAV4 markups in detail, but as a brief recap, Capitol Toyota in San Jose, California was adding $5,995 across the board to RAV4 models, while Stevens Creek Toyota, situated nearby, applied a $4,995 markup to all RAV4 models listed on their site. Sure, given the low supply and continuously high demand for RAV4 models, it's very likely these dealers got what they were asking, but have they ignored the bigger picture? If prices were stable at or at least near MSRP, many customers may have chosen to be patient, and await further builds to arrive. However, seeing heavily inflated prices would have likely driven customers away, right into the arms of dealers with Honda, Subaru, and Mazda emblems above their entryways. The Toyota RAV4 is a sales monster because it is affordable, reliable, and good. A production shortage, especially one of this magnitude, is bad for all crossover buyers, though, not just RAV4 customers. It encourages dealers to mark up the fewer RAV4 models they get, and as buyers shift to other models instead, it dries up that inventory as well, reducing incentives. Toyota meeting demand for the RAV4 should be good for all affordable vehicle buyers, but this ripple could be felt for years. Especially as it trickles down to the used market. King Harald of Norway will be laid to rest in a state funeral on 9 September, with his wife, Queen Sonja, expected to lead the congregation of international royals As Norway prepares to bid a final farewell to King Harald V, royals and world leaders from across the globe are set to gather in Oslo to celebrate the life of the late monarch. King Harald died on 28 August following hospitalisation with a blood infection, bringing to a close a remarkable 35-year reign that saw him become one of the most beloved figures in Norwegian public life. His state funeral will take place at Oslo Cathedral on 9 September, with thousands expected to pay their respects in the capital during the period of national mourning. Following the funeral, King Harald will be laid to rest in the Royal Mausoleum at Akershus Fortress, overlooking Oslo Fjord. An interview with Britain's Strictest Head, a tour of international schools and a celebration of 100 years of the Royal Ballet School: Tatler's education editor, Tori Cadogan, reveals what to expect from this year's guide, on sale 3rd September with the October issue For more than three decades, King Harald stood at the heart of Norwegian life. Affectionately known as the ‘people’s king’, he was celebrated for his ability to unite the country through moments of both celebration and hardship, championing LGBTQ+ rights and comforting the nation following the tragic 2011 terrorist attacks. His reign witnessed enormous social and cultural change, yet the King remained a reassuringly familiar presence, admired for his devotion to public service and his close relationship with the Norwegian people. The Norwegian royal family has been grieving for the late monarch following his death on 28 August Now, Oslo is preparing for one of the most significant royal occasions in recent royal history, as an extraordinary gathering of kings, queens, princes, princesses and political leaders arrives to pay tribute to the late monarch. The ceremony is expected to bring together the great and the good of the international royal world, many of whom shared decades-long friendships and family ties with King Harald. The occasion will also mark a deeply personal moment for the Norwegian royal family. King Haakon VIII, who succeeded his father following his death, will lead the family in mourning alongside Queen Mette-Marit and their daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, now first in line to the throne. European royal families have long been closely intertwined, and King Harald counted many of the continent’s monarchs among both his relatives and friends. His funeral will therefore be not only a major state occasion, but an unusually intimate gathering of a royal generation that has known one another for much of their lives. King Harald and Queen Sonja at Edinburgh Castle on a state visit to Great Britain in 1994 Among those confirmed to attend are King Frederik X and Queen Mary of Denmark, who have postponed their state visit to Belgium in order to travel to Oslo. King Willem-Alexander and Queen Máxima of the Netherlands will also attend, accompanied by Princess Beatrix and Catharina-Amalia, Princess of Orange, bringing three generations of the Dutch royal family together to pay their respects. From Japan, Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko are expected to represent the Imperial Family. From bidding farewell to time-travel smash Outlander to playing a ‘manifesting’ Mrs Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility, actress Caitríona Balfe is a busy woman. So much so that Dora Davies-Evitt had to hunt her down on holiday at an Irish castle… While the British royal family have not yet confirmed who will represent King Charles at the funeral, it may well be Princess Anne who travels to Oslo. The Princess Royal is, after all, godmother to the new King Haakon VIII. The funeral at Oslo Cathedral will offer one final opportunity to reflect on King Harald’s 35 years on the throne, and for Norway, and the royal world beyond it, to say goodbye. title: 2026 Cadillac Optiq-V Review: Premium Design, Premium Price, Mediocre Ride - The Drive
content:

Bottom line: The Cadillac Optiq-V offers luxury and power but lacks the engaging drive and efficiency expected at its price point. Modern car manufacturing is really something. Take the Chevrolet Equinox EV, a rather boring but totally competent electric commuter. Thanks to the modular nature of electric powertrains, General Motors can pop the lid off that SUV, pack in more powerful motors along with some other go-fast nuts and bolts, snap on a more stylish and luxurious body, and create this: The Cadillac Optiq-V. It’s a $70,000 version of a vehicle that Chevy sells for half that. So, we started with one of the most affordable and popular EVs in America, and we ended up in the territory of a bona fide high-performance electric SUV. The Optiq-V makes 519 horsepower and 650 lb-ft of torque. It has massive six-piston Brembo brakes up front, stiffer anti-roll bars, and adaptive dampers; it also completes the 0-60 dash in 3.5 seconds. The problem is, I didn’t really enjoy driving it. And that sucks all the wind from the sails of a vehicle like this, wearing the badge that it does, which is typically an initial for fun. An ordinary Cadillac Optiq starts at $52,695 and is powered by a 315-hp motor on the rear axle. For about another $16,000, you can get into the Optiq-V, which considerably boosts not only the power and poise in the corners but also style and luxury. I think this is a handsome SUV with a nice profile, even if it’s not as dramatic as the Lyriq’s. The Nimbus Metallic paint on my tester here is a bit lighter than I’d probably go for, but it’s unique and still plays off the deeper hues of the interior trim and the graphic pattern along the C-pillar. I’m pleased to report that the panel is not opaque when viewed from inside the car and functions as a typical tiny quarter window. This particular example came in at $79,270, which is indeed a lot of money. Part of that is because of the paint, which is a $725 option. The $2,555 Charging and Convenience package upgrades the onboard AC charger to 19.2 kW, from the regular 11.5 kW. This has an adverse effect on range, unfortunately, reducing it to all but 250 miles with this configuration, down from the regular 278 miles. More on that later. Rather, the bulk of extra dollars and cents comes courtesy of the $5,500 (!) carbon fiber exterior package, which clads the trim, including that rather prominent rear diffuser, in the stuff. It probably goes without saying, but I don’t think this option adds much of consequence to the vehicle. Here’s the thing about the Optiq-V: Cadillac engineers say they seriously touched every part of this car, well beyond its powertrain, and I fully believe them. It is quick in a straight line, of course, but it’s also rigid, rides confidently but never punishingly so, and can hang on with loads of grip in high-speed corners. But of course, like many electric SUVs, this one is heavy, and I don’t think enough was done to make it feel otherwise. Interestingly, the steering rack was one of the aspects Cadillac tweaked specifically for the Optiq-V, but they didn’t go far enough—the ratio is just too slow. Couple that with the effort required to turn it, and its unnecessarily large size, and you’re left with a vehicle that paradoxically can hold its own in the twisties, but almost discourages you from finding out how well. Again, it’s not that this thing doesn’t corner flat, because it very much does, but the disconnect between objective agility and perceived agility almost surprises you when you push it. You almost have to remind yourself that it wants to and is engineered to be driven hard, and I assume Blackwing owners don’t encounter that phenomenon. In less dynamic situations, the Optiq-V felt every bit the luxury EV it’s billed as behind the wheel, with a ride that lets you feel the texture of the road but is never too harsh, superb sound deadening, and seamless blending between regeneration and friction braking. I still turned off regen—it’s become a GM tradition for me, after all, as I can’t stand the strength with which their cars make the world stop turning the moment you lift your foot off the throttle—but the option is there if you want it. And even if I wish the steering was livelier, it is still nevertheless very accurate. In some respects, the Optiq’s cabin represents everything Cadillac is doing well right now. It’s elegantly simple with fantastic materials, from the heather tweed dashboard upholstery to the matte-metallic pop of electric blue that runs from the driver’s-side A-pillar to just beneath the center stack. The fit and finish of the Optiq-V’s interior is unquestionably my favorite thing about it. It would be nicer if it were just a bit more intuitive to operate. I’ve whined about CarPlay’s omission in enough reviews of GM EVs, so we won’t retread that ground, but even the climate vents are hard to direct with any kind of purpose. You can’t see the vanes on the vents themselves, and they’re really slender, so you kind of just have to yank the knobs around until a thin blade of air eventually brushes against you, which is never as obvious as you’d think. This trim comes with massaging seats, though they offer exactly one pretty underwhelming mode, and the dial they’re linked up to on the front door cards is very confusing to operate. The steering wheel, in addition to being too large as we discussed, is entirely controlled through capacitive keys, which is frustrating. And while I know GM’s infotainment system has received high marks from some, I always find myself wishing it were more customizable and that it let me modify gauge cluster widgets with fewer taps. Although the lack of a frunk is frustrating, there’s plenty of space in here, and rear-seat passengers should be quite comfortable. Compared to the Equinox EV, legroom in the back is trimmed ever so slightly due to the fancier, thicker front seats, but the Equinox was already working with a ton of second-row real estate as it is, so this isn’t a problem at all. Range is where the argument against the Optiq-V in particular, compared to other trims, gets pretty damning. Technically, this vehicle can deliver up to 278 miles of range, depending on how it’s configured. Mine was limited to 250, which is simply not enough for a considerably sized SUV you’d haul the family in. That’s Cadillac’s official estimation, and that’s pretty much exactly what I got, never seeing better than 3 miles per kilowatt-hour. At a time when more and more EVs, even fast ones, are landing in the high 3s or even breaking the 4 mi/kWh mark, efficiency needs to improve. Of course, the ordinary Optiqs don’t have this problem. The rear-wheel-drive model is rated to return a very respectable 317 miles on a full charge, while the dual-motor non-V flavor calls for 303 miles. Making matters worse, the Optiq inherits the Equinox EV’s peculiar charging behavior, which limits you to 150 kW at a Level 3 DC fast charger, compared to the 250 kW or so that the Hyundai Ioniq 5 achieves. For a bargain, entry-level EV, 150 kW is totally acceptable. For an $80,000 one, though, that performance becomes harder to swallow. At least there’s an integrated NACS port, which means you don’t have to think twice about stopping at a Tesla Supercharger. Cadillac’s mission to take a basic electric crossover and transform it into a grand tourer with the Optiq-V is admirable. Yet, while I take no issue with its luxury credentials, it lacks the vigor you’d hope for at its price and concedes far too much range. This isn’t a question of “Who is this car for?” because the market has long since proven that there’s an audience for premium SUVs with some sporting pretense. The problem is that Cadillac hasn’t nailed the sporty part of the equation, while other automakers—from Hyundai to Porsche—have. Cadillac provided The Drive with a seven-day loan of this vehicle for the purpose of writing this review. The Cadillac Optiq-V feels premium but doesn’t drive with the liveliness that the label commands, and is frustratingly inefficient on a full battery compared to other trims. title: V162: Crafting Joy With Anya Taylor-Joy - V Magazine
content: From the world of Dune to the high-stakes suspense of Lucky, the actor is turning the page to a bold new chapter. Dressed in bespoke paper creations by fashion’s latest visionaries, the actor reminds us that the most compelling narratives are crafted with equal parts imagination and style From the world of Dune to the high-stakes suspense of Lucky, the actor is turning the page to a bold new chapter. Dressed in bespoke paper creations by fashion’s latest visionaries, the actor reminds us that the most compelling narratives are crafted with equal parts imagination and style The nature of paper is that it’s always in a state of becoming: a story, a journal, a script, and now, a dress. Few know this better than Anya Taylor-Joy, whose own love of the written word has inspired a monumental creative dialogue between V, photographer Nick Knight, stylist Anna Trevelyan, a coterie of designers, and Montblanc, known for their own dedication to the life of a page. For the September issue of V, the likes of Matthew David Andrews, Noel Stewart, Jenny Beattie, AGRO Studio, Macy Grimshaw, Thevxlley, Gaurav Gupta, Miguel Castro Freitas for Mugler, and Zac Posen for GapStudio produced original dresses made entirely of paper for Taylor-Joy to wear. In a world that’s increasingly so digital, there’s ever more beauty in the tactile. This collaboration becomes a love letter to fashion, punctuated with the words “I love you my angel,” written by Taylor-Joy’s own mother in Montblanc’s Meisterstück pen when she visited the set of the photoshoot. No matter the folds and creases of life, Taylor-Joy has come to see the world through pages of her own, whether as a longtime keeper of journals; an avid reader; on scripts she helps bring to life as an actor in films like Dune’s third installment, arriving later this year; or as a producer, on series like Lucky and movies like Sacrifice. As she continues writing the chapters of her life, Anya Taylor-Joy spoke to dear friend Miley Cyrus for V about building a character, escaping the pressures of fame, managing expectations, and finding the beauty in one’s imperfections. MILEY CYRUS: What is it that makes you fall in love with a character? ANYA TAYLOR-JOY: It feels like less of a choice, more of an instinct. My body figures it out before I do–I start sitting differently, speaking the words aloud in a new voice. I believe every character has things to teach you. MC: Does music matter to you in movies? Can a score totally make or break a film for you? ATJ: Absolutely. I LOVE film scores and soundtracks. I make my own playlists for jobs but the few times I’ve been given a theme for a character whilst shooting, it totally changes the game. MC: What was it about Lucky that made you go, “I have to do this”? ATJ: At first, the opportunity to fully produce it alongside such impressive collaborators was hugely appealing but I didn’t want to jump in unless I felt I had something to add. Luckily, reading the book I immediately saw the texture of the world and through the empathy I felt for her, I knew this was material I could sink my teeth into and expand. MC: You executive produced Lucky and Sacrifice. What made you want to get more involved from the ground up? Was it fun exercising both sides of your brain? I always think of it as the head and the heart…the boss side and the creative side. ATJ: Exactly. It honestly felt like something I had always been doing, it just now had a job title. I’ve never been able to not think of the project as a whole–I’m obsessed with how something moves, feels, sounds. It’s all storytelling. As a producer you get to help design the world your character lives in. I’m in love with all aspects of filmmaking so to have the ability to play in all the different sandboxes is a thrill.MC: When you step back into a world like Dune, how do you keep it fun for yourself? I imagine there’s so much pressure on a film that big, and I know you love to have a good time, so how do you make sure you don’t lose that? ATJ: I’ve never let that be a concern. Of course I hope fans will be happy with the end result, but I never forget that I myself am a fan. Of the world, the filmmaker, the character. I approach every job the same–with complete commitment to the present, an open heart and wild curiosity. It’s all an adventure! MC: I know travel is such a huge part of your life, and unlike me, you actually love being away from home. What’s one of your favorite places you’ve ever been? And what’s the one thing you always pack besides your hot husband? ATJ: Ooooh, I loved trekking with gorillas in Rwanda. Africa in general is extraordinary. Japan is exquisite. On Dune, I did a couple of side quests to Austria and South Korea. My blessing and my curse is I always travel with an insane amount of books. Nearly a full suitcase. Wish I could get behind a Kindle, but nothing beats holding a physical copy in your hand. MC: Dune has one of those fan bases that’s so passionate. Do you ever think about expectations? And whose opinion matters most to you? Is there someone in your life you’re still secretly trying to impress? ATJ: Oh wow. That cuts deep. I think I’m still trying to impress myself? I have absurdly high standards that can be exhausting at times. Not so much for other people but personally. I care so much about the creation that I want to make sure I’ve given it my best. Growing up has meant I’ve learned that sometimes perfection is in letting go. MC: Fame is part of the job, and it exposes parts of our lives that have nothing to do with the work. How have you learned to protect the parts of yourself that are just yours? ATJ: If anything, I think I’ve protected myself too much. It took me a minute to not feel hunted, to not want to hide. I’ve learned to take things less seriously by choosing which opinions actually matter to me and which are based on very little information at all. MC: What else outside of acting has been inspiring you lately? What are you finding yourself wanting to make outside of film? ATJ: Travel! Music. Older films. Nature. Clothessss. MC: I love that you journal. Has writing always been your way of making sense of your emotions and everything going on in your head? ATJ: Absolutely. It started first with wanting to remember my dreams. I’ve always had an active dream life–sometimes it feels more real than this one! Writing is such a sanctuary. Even if you don’t see the value in what you’re writing in the moment, with time you’ll notice little clues. Oscar Wilde wrote, “I never travel without my diary. One should always have something sensational to read on the train.” MC: What’s one of your favorite looks you’ve ever worn? Mine is obviously the Bob Mackie you wore at my Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony. You looked so gorg. ATJ: Thanks, angel. Any time I’ve worn Bob it’s been special. I wore a butter yellow Dior Haute Couture gown to my first Emmys with a low, low back and a huge canary yellow train. That one came in a dream and to see it come to life so beautifully was magic. MC: You have such a unique look. Did you ever have an awkward phase, or a time where you felt unsure in your own skin? ATJ: Oh yes, haha. I still do! I think that’s one of the lessons of life; we spend so much time analysing and trying to force our physical bodies to comply to whatever the current beauty standard is that we forget to enjoy its very existence. Whilst it still creeps up, I’m done with that. I’m way too grateful for the wonders it allows me to experience and the beauty it helps me produce. It’s my vehicle for fun. MC: When you think about everything that’s still ahead, what genuinely excites you the most that we wouldn’t expect? ATJ: Expanding my unjaded heart. Getting sillier. Feeling everything. And stretching beyond my imagination. ATJ: Hardddd. It’s a toss-up between a snow leopard, a hummingbird, and a killer whale. title: League of Women Voters of Massachusetts v. Trump - American Civil Liberties Union
content: On March 31, 2026, President Trump issued a sweeping Executive Order titled "Ensuring Citizen Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections," seeking once again to seize control of election administration from Congress and the states. The Order directs federal agencies to compile lists of U.S. citizens and transmit them to states before every election, directs the U.S. Postal Service -- an independent agency established by Congress -- to create a list of "approved" mail voters, and instructs USPS to refuse to deliver ballots from voters not on that federally created list. If implemented, the Order would threaten the ability of millions of eligible citizens to cast their ballots, particularly military members, overseas citizens, the elderly, recently naturalized citizens, and voters with disabilities who rely on mail voting. By completing this form, I agree to receive occasional emails per the terms of the ACLU's privacy statement. The Constitution gives Congress and the states — not the President — the power to regulate elections. Despite this, President Trump's March 31, 2026 Executive Order attempts to impose a sweeping new federal regime over mail-in and absentee voting nationwide. The Order directs the Department of Homeland Security to compile lists of citizens from federal databases — including Social Security Administration records and immigration data — and transmit those lists to states before every federal election. It then directs USPS to refuse to deliver mail-in or absentee ballots from any voter who does not appear on a federally created enrollment list. It also threatens states with non-delivery of their voters' ballots unless those states submit lists of eligible mail voters to USPS at least 60 days before each election. The ACLU, ACLU of Massachusetts, and co-counsel voting rights advocate partners have sued to block President Trump's Order. We proudly represent the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts, the League of Women Voters, Association of Americans Resident Overseas (AARO), U.S. Vote Foundation, OCA - Asian Pacific American Advocates (OCA), and Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc. This Executive Order is President Trump's second attempt to seize control of federal elections by executive fiat, issued despite injunctions from three separate federal courts blocking a previous 2025 Executive Order on similar grounds. Plaintiffs bring six claims: the Order violates the constitutional separation of powers; it is ultra vires because it commandeers USPS in violation of Congress's postal statutes; it violates the Tenth Amendment and principles of federalism by coercing states to alter their election laws; it unconstitutionally burdens the right to vote; it violates Section 11(a) of the Voting Rights Act by directing USPS to refuse to deliver lawful ballots to eligible voters; and it violates the Privacy Act by requiring the rushed, non-consensual compilation and dissemination of inaccurate personal data about millions of Americans without the required public notice and comment. Update: On August 27, 2026, the District Court temporarily blocked USPS from enforcing key provisions of a finalized mail-ballot rule for the November 2026 election. The federal government appealed and asked the First Circuit to stay that relief pending appeal. The District Court is now considering Plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction that would block enforcement of the rule through the November election.
